Breaking: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer claims it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he notes he has identified the next massive shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his manufacturer Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Recent findings suggest that andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having stated that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Industry observers note that ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having stated that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of owners.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

In a recent development, I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Industry observers note that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and remarked, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

In a recent development, the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

In a recent development, ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

Sources indicate that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand latest model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

It has been revealed that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For substantial data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very promptly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Latest tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an vital piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is notable, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

In a recent development, for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Industry observers note that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

Recent findings suggest that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Recent findings suggest that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these concerns more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a organization approaches Landing AI and indicates it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

Sources indicate that one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and enhancement the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

Recent findings suggest that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

According to recent reports, ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we get older, things change, and while I don't necessarily recommend that someone swap their entire routine just because of a number, there are certain factors to consider, especially as you pass the 40 mark.

This applies to both men and women, but particularly women, whose hormones change with perimenopause and menopause, which impacts lean muscle mass and joint and bone health. But regardless, sarcopenia (the age-related, progressive loss of muscle mass, strength, and physical function) begins to accelerate through the 40s and 50s and still applies to everyone.

For that reason, there are a few tweaks we can make to help the transition, and I'm going to lay them out for you below using my experience as a personal trainer and fitness editor.

Sources indicate that I absolutely refuse to change someone's gym program just because of a number. Instead, I listen to the client and their goals, potential health conditions, injuries, or life experiences, and I also program to my clients' abilities and scale accordingly.

In fact, I train my 72-year-old dad like he's 30 years younger and he's stronger and more mobile than ever.

It has been revealed that that remarked, people over 40 may notice slower recovery times and changes to joint mobility, strength, or muscle mass. This is a period of time when I think building and maintaining muscle becomes extremely important for function, balance and performance.

For some, it may be possible to remain doing high-impact cardio or HIIT routines, but for many, I see a gradual shift toward low-impact routines such as Pilates or yoga and strength training, which may involve lifting weights at home or in the gym.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Changes to hormones and lower collagen levels mean muscles may take slightly longer to repair and recover from workouts, which makes overtraining easier to accidentally fall into.

Lower collagen levels can also impact your joints, which play a vital role in mobility; tendons and ligaments will also lose elasticity with age, which means you'll need to really focus on proper warm-ups and cool-downs to maintain range of motion without injury or strain.

Alongside sarcopenia, which I mentioned earlier, bone density decreases into your 40s and 50s as well, impacting balance and strength, which can make the likelihood of injuries or falls higher.

It has been revealed that sam Hopes is a level 3 qualified trainer, a level 2 Reiki practitioner and fitness editor at Tom's Guide. She is also right now undertaking her Yoga For Athletes training course.

Sam has written for various fitness brands and websites over the years and has experience across brands at Future, such as Live Science, Fit&Well, Coach, and T3.

Having coached at fitness studios like F45 and Virgin Active and taken on both 1:1 and group, Sam now primarily teaches outdoor bootcamps, bodyweight, and kettlebells.

She also coaches mobility and flexibility classes several times a week.

Sam has completed two mixed doubles Hyrox competitions in London and the Netherlands and finished her first doubles attempt in 1:11.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This paper constructs an unconditional, zero-error Las Vegas algorithm on a single fixed uniform classical multitape Turing machine $\mathcal{M}$ that computes the exact complete prime factorization $N = \prod_{1 \le i \le k} p_i^{e_i}$ ($p_1 < \dots < p_k$ prime, $e_i \ge 1$) of every integer $N \ge 2$ given in standard binary representation, halting with probability $1$ over its read-once fair coin flips, in worst-case expected time $L_N[1/3, 105]$ and worst-case deterministic workspace $L_N[1/3, 40]$, where.

$$L_x(\alpha, c) := \exp!\bigl(c,(\ln x)^\alpha (\ln\ln x)^{1-\alpha}\bigr)$$.

and $T(N) \le L_N[\alpha, c]$ means.

$$ \limsup_{N \to \infty} \frac{\ln \max(1, T(N))}{(\ln N)^\alpha (\ln\ln N)^{1-\alpha}} \le c. $$.

Every prime factor in the output is certified deterministically via Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena primality testing and direct multiplication against $N$, with effectively computable constants and no unproven number-theoretic hypotheses. A complete, unconditional, Mathlib-only Lean 4 (v4.35.0) formalization of the entire proof has also been completed and will be released in a companion submission.

This paper and its Lean 4 formalization were entirely obtained by Cogentic (arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.40324), an agentic framework for mathematical discovery, using Gemini 4 as the base model. There was no human interaction other than the initial prompt for Cogentic to generate a full proof and formalization. The Cogentic harness was built by Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, and Di Wang (Google Research and Google DeepMind).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that imagine creating your own budgeting app, meal planner or productivity tool by just describing what you want. Now imagine opening that app directly from your computer without digging through your chat history.

In a recent development, that's exactly what Anthropic is making possible with its latest Claude revision. The firm announced on Tuesday that users can now turn Claude Artifacts into desktop apps for Mac and Windows, complete with their own icons, dedicated windows, and notifications.

Perhaps the best part is that you don't need a paid Claude subscription or any coding experience to get started.

Recent findings suggest that the feature is at the moment rolling out in beta across all Claude aims, including the free tier. And while AI chatbots have been able to build interactive tools for some time, this patch makes those creations considerably more practical for everyday use.

Until now, one of the drawbacks of building an interactive tool with Claude was that using it meant going back into Claude. Giving those creations a permanent place on your desktop changes that experience.

You could create a custom app that helps you stay focused throughout the workday, a family chore tracker or even a holiday shopping organizer that keeps tabs on your budget.

Here are five app ideas and prompts worth trying:.

Anthropic employees have already used the feature to create everything from a layered image editor to a computer performance monitor.

Apps can also work with services you've connected to Claude, opening up possibilities for more personalized tools.

Getting started doesn't require downloading a separate coding tool or setting up an API key.

Download or patch the Claude desktop app for Mac or Windows.

Describe the app you want Claude to build.

Try out the resulting Artifact and ask Claude to make any necessary changes.

Open the Share menu and select Install as app.

Review and confirm any requested permissions.

You can continue refining your creation through Claude, and changes to the original Artifact will carry over to the installed app.

According to recent reports, there are several limitations to keep in mind. These apps aren't completely independent of Claude. You'll need an internet connection and an active Claude login to open them, and any AI requests they make count toward your existing usage limits.

Not every Artifact can be installed, either. Claude's standard documents, presentations and spreadsheets are among the exclusions.

Industry observers note that security is another consideration. Anthropic doesn't review apps before installation, and certain permissions can let an app modify or delete files on your computer.

I'd recommend sticking with the default permissions unless your app genuinely needs additional access. Be especially careful about installing creations shared by others.

One of the things I find most compelling about this update is that it gives everyday users a reason to experiment with vibe coding beyond the novelty of building something with AI.

Think about how many times you've downloaded an app only to discover that half the features are locked behind a subscription, or that it doesn't work quite the way you'd like.

On the eve of Thanksgiving at the NFL halftime show, U2 performed the Dolly Parton and Bono duet, “Torn,” as the country great’s image was projected on screens surrounding the stage.

It was a poignant moment during the show, as the song was the final vocal recording of Parton’s seven-decade career. The track appears on U2’s recently debuted album, Carnaval de Luz. While Parton, who shares writing credits for the song with the band and Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid, originally wrote “Torn” around a story of a woman trying to choose between two men, Bono and McDaid rewrote the lyrics around a mother watching her family divided. “You name the location,” Bono told Rolling Stone for U2’s recent cover story, “but everyone knows what it is.… People say in the U.S. now, people are scared to go into Thanksgiving.”.

Sources indicate that parton, who died in August at age 80, recorded her part on the album’s closing track in June. “When she got ill,” Bono said, “she got out of her bed to sing this song. And you can hear that. Beyoncé performed at Netflix’s first NFL game on Christmas Day 2024, while Snoop Dogg took the stage last year.

During U2’s performance on during Wednesday’s show at Sofi Stadium, the band was joined by a massive marching choir and the Womack Sisters, who were recently nominated for Best Fresh Artist and Best Traditional R&B Performance (“If I Let You”) at the 69th Grammys.

  • Sources indicate that I've tested all three of these headphones — and a boatload more of their closest competitors — so I can help you choose the correct pair.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with MSRPs of $549, $449, and $459, respectively, the Apple AirPods Max 2, Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2nd Gen, and the Sony WH-1000XM6 aren't exactly cheap. That's why Black Friday deals are so great, as they're all on sale right now.

Sources indicate that I've tested all three of these headphones — and a boatload more of their closest competitors — so I can help you choose the correct pair. Do you value sound quality? ANC? Comfort? Extra features?

I'll go through everything the AirPods Max 2, Bose QC Ultra, and Sony XM6 offer right now — let's figure this out together. Which headphones should you buy this Black Friday?

It has been revealed that if you're an Apple user, there are no better headphones than the AirPods Max 2 (at this price, of course). With gorgeously detailed sound and an expansive soundscape, I'm happy to overlook the slightly heavy head-feel.

Recent findings suggest that the Bose QuietComfort Ultra are ideal headphones if you value comfort and ANC over anything else — or, of course, if you have a predilection for bass. These headphones don't sound as detailed as Apple or Sony's versions, but they pack a major punch.

Sony's WH-1000XM6 are great headphones for most people, with clear call quality, proficient ANC, and detailed sound. They're the best all-rounder for both iPhone and Android customers.

It has been revealed that we've reached the point with Bluetooth headphones where you're probably not going to be disappointed by any pair. I've tested super-budget options worthy of making a "best of" list (Soundcore Space 2, CMF by Nothing Headphone Pro, both $99), just as I've tested these three behemoths.

According to recent reports, there's no one "best": it all depends on your personal preferences. For the purpose of this article, I re-tested all three headphones with three of my go-to testing tracks.

The AirPods Max 2 have the most dynamic and exciting sound quality. "space cadet" by sim0ne is an energetic hard house track with euphoric '90s pianos and expansive hi-hats layered under a pitched-up female vocal. The tick-tock synths tinkled in the background with energy and zeal, while the kick drum pummelled the low-end with control.

Rock also sounds excellent on the AirPods Max 2; "Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" by Deftones starts with a grating guitar, which came through dynamically on the Max 2. The crashing cymbals at the top of the soundstage didn't wash out the grunge instrumentation, and although I can see the percussion growing tiresome after a long listening session, there's vibrancy in the soundscape.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

"Vogue (Q-Sound Mix" by Madonna is excellent for testing spatial imaging. On the AirPods Max 2, Madonna's vocals came through in each earcup independently, with no warping or confusion in the stereo. The subtle synth bassline rounded out the track delicately, without overwhelming the mids or vocals.

Industry observers note that the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2nd Gen are more for bassheads. If you really like a punchy, propulsive low-end, I'd recommend the Bose.

I tested the Bose QC Ultra with the same three songs as the AirPods Max 2. "space cadet" by sim0ne wasn't as expansive or detailed as the AirPods, but the kick drum hit so much harder. As soon as the chorus broke, the synth bassline and drum machine took control of the track. The bass pulsed in my ears. sim0ne's pitched-up vocals were still clear, but the bass was the true star of the show.

In a recent development, "Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" benefited from the same elevated bass — the crunchy, almost too-sharp opening guitar gave way to a truly raucous verse. The bass carried the entire track, somewhat pushing the percussion to the soundstage's edge, but didn't overpower the vocals. Anyone into rock or grunge would seriously love these headphones.

Lastly, I played "Vogue (Q-Symphony Mix)" to test stereo imaging. Bose's "Immersive" feature really came into play here: I could hear the track coming from behind me, beside me, in front of me. I'd say this immersion was even better than the AirPods Max 2's — my brain was well and truly tricked. And when that bassline came in? I'm gone. It's over. I'm on the dancefloor, bye!

Industry observers note that last but certainly not least, let's chat about the Sony WH-1000XM6. These are famous the best "all-rounder" headphones: they're detailed and expansive, bassy yet clear, and are the best of all worlds.

Sources indicate that once again, I played "space cadet" by sim0ne. This track was bright and fun, with a whole load of clarity across the treble and mid-range. Every snare and hi-hat coruscated across the soundstage without overpowering those lovely tick-tock synth notes. The euphoric pianos were lovely and detailed, and when the bassline kicked in, it kicked in. Obviously, it wasn't as hard-hitting as the Bose, but the XM6s prioritize clarity and detail over booming bass.

Sources indicate that heavier genres fared well, too. "Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)" by Deftones pounded through the headphones with the ferocity of a runaway freight train. Bass and guitars snarled in my ears without overpowering the vocals. Although the bass, again, didn't have quite as much boom as the Bose headphones, these are detail-focused instead.

It has been revealed that finally, I played "Vogue (Q-Symphony Mix)" to test spatial imaging. Madonna's voice danced around my head, making me feel like the music was coming from everywhere. Fingers snapped in my left ear, and bongos drummed in my right ear. I will say the Sonys weren't as truly immersive as the Bose and AirPods, but this was still a phenomenal performance.

It has been revealed that the AirPods Max 2 are 13 ounces; Bose QC Ultra 9.3 ounces; Sony WX6 8.96 ounces. If you're going to be wearing your headphones all day, I'd recommend the Bose or Sony.

Although I can wear the AirPods Max 2 for at least a few hours without needing to take them off, and the mesh headband alleviates a lot of weight, if you need as little head fatigue as possible, I'd go for the Bose or Sony.

Especially if you're a frequent flyer — the Bose QC Ultra are unbeatable for flights. You won't be able to hear the engine, other passengers, or even your own thoughts with these. It's a win all round.

Industry observers note that you won't be disappointed by ANC on any of these headphones. I've worn all three while working, running errands across the city, and in noisy environments like bars.

If you're wearing these headphones while working in an office, all three will minimize ambient sounds like keyboards clacking and mice clicking. I found the best to be the Bose QuietComfort Ultra, but the AirPods and Sony also cocooned me in a vacuum of quiet.

For really loud environments, or if you have noisy neighbors or construction outside your house, I'd recommend the Bose QuietComfort Ultra. While the AirPods Max 2 and Sony WH-1000XM6 are excellent, Dr. Bose literally invented ANC — and it indicates.

If you want even more information, I have a full Apple AirPods Max 2 vs Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen vs Sony WH-1000XM6 for your reading pleasure.

According to recent reports, if you're an Apple user, there are no better headphones than the AirPods Max 2 (at this price, of course). With gorgeously detailed sound and an expansive soundscape, I'm happy to overlook the slightly heavy head-feel.

It has been revealed that the Bose QuietComfort Ultra are ideal headphones if you value comfort and ANC over anything else — or, of course, if you have a predilection for bass. These headphones don't sound as detailed as Apple or Sony's versions, but they pack a major punch.

According to recent reports, sony's WH-1000XM6 are great headphones for most people, with clear call quality, proficient ANC, and detailed sound. They're the best all-rounder for both iPhone and Android owners.

For most people, I would recommend the Sony WH-1000XM6.

For bass lovers or frequent travelers, I'd go for the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen.

For iPhone users who value dynamic sound, grab the Apple AirPods Max 2.

Because I have an iPhone and MacBook, I would personally buy the AirPods Max 2.

#200185. Lincoln’s Thanksgiving Lesson For Us Now: Don’t Claim Victory Yet

Lincoln’s Thanksgiving Lesson For Us Now: Don’t Claim Victory Yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one hundred sixty-three years ago, Americans gathered for what began an unbroken annual tradition: Thanksgiving.
  • According to recent reports, some Americans will come to the table this year carrying wounds of their own.
  • In a recent development, some observers have called this month’s midterms a “Gettysburg moment.” The comparison is apt, but not for the reason most people think.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one hundred sixty-three years ago, Americans gathered for what began an unbroken annual tradition: Thanksgiving. It came one week after Abraham Lincoln stood in a field at Gettysburg to dedicate a cemetery. In three days of fighting there that July, 50,000 Americans had been killed, wounded, captured, or gone missing. That summer, after Gettysburg and Vicksburg, Lincoln had called for a day of thanksgiving for the Union’s victories. By fall, he asked for something more. He did not ask a grieving country to set its losses aside. He asked it to give thanks despite the losses, to remember the “widows, orphans, mourners, or sufferers,” and to work to “heal the wounds of the nation.”.

According to recent reports, some Americans will come to the table this year carrying wounds of their own. And amid a common narrative that Americans are hopelessly divided, many may feel a bit lighter because the nation came together to hold free and fair elections this month. Still, many will sit across the table from people who view the results differently.

In a recent development, some observers have called this month’s midterms a “Gettysburg moment.” The comparison is apt, but not for the reason most people think. Gettysburg was not a turning point on July 3, 1863, when the guns went quiet. It became one in the hard months that followed, because of what ordinary people did next.

When Lincoln delivered his address at Gettysburg that November, he didn’t take credit. He didn’t use the moment as an opportunity to win a factional political debate. Instead, he reminded the country of its core values and focused on the unfinished work ahead. Lincoln gave us a lesson for our times about what to do with a moment of reckoning. He came to dedicate a cemetery, and instead of taking a victory lap, he used his brief address to look ahead:.

Industry observers note that “It is for us the living . . . to be dedicated here to the unfinished work which they who fought here have thus far so nobly advanced.”.

With those words, Lincoln passed the work to the people.

The hardest fighting was still ahead. When Lincoln came to Gettysburg, the war’s outcome was far from settled, and Gettysburg had not yet acquired its reputation as the turning point. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

According to recent reports, it became one because of what those still living did next. In the months after Gettysburg, the South didn’t simply give up just because their defeat seemed inevitable. Instead, it dug in, fighting harder to make victory for the Union as costly as possible. But, Union soldiers kept fighting in a series of battles — some of the bloodiest of the war — slowly but steadfastly liberating parts of the South from enslavement. By 1865, the grim work paid off and the Union had prevailed.

In 2026, we are standing now where the crowd stood when Lincoln came to Gettysburg: after the battle, before anyone knows how the war ends and with grueling work ahead.

In a recent development, in 2021, after January 6, the United States was first added to a global list of “backsliding” democracies. The slide has since sharply accelerated. Trump has pardoned the people who stormed the Capitol, sent troops into American cities, sought to suppress the right to vote, and went to war with Iran without Congress.

According to recent reports, but as a Republican-controlled Congress abandoned its constitutional duty to check the president, and powerful law firms, universities, and media companies capitulated, ordinary people stepped forward. Residents filled the streets to protect neighbors from armed federal agents. Millions joined “No Kings” marches in all 50 states. People and state attorneys general filed more than 900 lawsuits and won orders protecting people’s rights.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, despite threats from the White House and its allies, Americans voted. Roughly 49 percent of eligible voters cast ballots, the second-highest midterm turnout since 1914. Power shifted in Texas. Mississippi elected its first Black senator since Reconstruction. Kansas sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 94 years. Related Content Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Postponed For Weather The Man Who Broke the Texas Democratic Party to Save It Stephen Miller Wants to Win Back Young Men. It Might Not Be So Easy ‘Dare Him to Veto It’: Democrats Are Ready to Push for Real Reform.

It has been revealed that since the election, the political conversation has fixated on what latest Democratic majorities should do with their power, who might run in 2028, and whether the Republican Party will reform itself. These are crucial questions, but some of this discourse falls back into a habit the media and political classes must break: It treats Americans as spectators. This election was won by people who would not sit on the sidelines: voters who indicated up despite threats, neighbors who organized, Americans who refused to accept that the outcome was already decided. The most important question now is not what political parties will do, it is what we, the people, do next.

Democracy is not decided on Election Day. It is built between elections — by people, not parties — in communities, courtrooms, statehouses, and school boards. And the gains voters made at the polls can be taken apart there, too, quietly, while no one is watching.

In a recent development, we are already seeing this. In Texas, outgoing officeholders have met behind closed doors to discuss stripping power from the lieutenant governor voters just chose. U.S. Senate Republicans are racing to confirm lifetime judges before they lose their majority in January. And the president named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff days after the election, while his administration threatens members of Congress with criminal prosecution.

No ballot will stop any of that. What can is what produced this month’s results: people who refused to look away — the plaintiff who signed a lawsuit, the neighbor on the sidewalk, the friend calling their lawmakers, the volunteer knocking doors.

We must pay attention after the cameras leave. Lame-duck sessions, rule changes, and quiet appointments are where hard-won results get undone. The threats from the executive branch will continue through 2028, and the lawsuits and movements that held the line will be needed more, not less.

According to recent reports, we must stay focused. Americans want a government that delivers — costs they can afford, healthcare, safe air travel — and we should insist on it. We should also reject a false choice between accountability and a government that delivers. Values-based accountability is not retribution. It is how a democracy highlights that no one is above the law, and it is part of delivering for people. We also should stay focused on longer-term changes that the nation and the people need to avoid a backslide in the future. Even if bolder changes like the U.S Supreme Court or passing comprehensive voter reform won’t get past this president’s veto, the next two years are the time to build the case for them. The people should not let political gridlock curtail their demands for a changed future. Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 U2 Perform Dolly Parton's Final Recording During NFL Halftime Show Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys The Country Song About Losing Your Virginity That Became an Enduring Hit.

It has been revealed that we must build community. This fall, voters rejected culture wars and runaway oligarchs. Elon Musk alone spent an estimated $474 million to elect Republicans. In Texas, Republicans poured at least $78 million into anti-trans ads against Senator-elect James Talarico, nearly half of the GOP’s ad spending in the race. Texas flipped anyway. Voters revealed they could see past division, and that they weren’t for sale. We should expect attempts to divide us to accelerate. The ties we build across differences are the infrastructure of self-government, and they hold only if we keep using and building them.

According to recent reports, gratitude and grief are two sides of the same coin. Lincoln understood that, and he asked a wounded nation to hold both. This Thanksgiving, they call us to the same thing: to find the grit and grace to keep going, and to make the fighting chance the midterms gave the people our nation’s watershed moment. Some 15,000 were in the crowd at Gettysburg. Lincoln wasn’t speaking only to his generals, his Cabinet or Congress. He was speaking to the people. The work was theirs. Now it is ours.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alarms are one of the most vital iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

It has been revealed that have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

According to recent reports, I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

According to recent reports, iOS 27 has two upcoming sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a upcoming volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you strategy to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

It has been revealed that december is shaping up to be another busy month for Paramount+, with plenty of newly introduced movies and shows arriving just in time for the holidays. Whether you’re looking for a gripping new series to get stuck into, a significant-screen film you missed the first time around or something festive to watch during the Christmas break, there’s plenty to keep an eye on.

Industry observers note that as always, I’ll be keeping this guide updated with everything fresh on Paramount+ throughout December 2026, including original series, returning favorites and movies. I’ll also highlight the biggest releases worth adding to your watchlist, so you don’t have to spend ages scrolling through the library to find something good. So, here’s everything coming to Paramount+ this month.

Industry observers note that one of the first massive releases coming to Paramount+ is “By Any Means,” a historical crime thriller inspired by real events surrounding organized crime and the civil rights movement in 1960s America. Mark Wahlberg plays a notorious Colombo crime family hitman who also spent years working as an FBI informant. The film takes some creative liberties with its historical characters and events, but there’s plenty of fascinating real-world material behind the story. It also has striking visuals and strong performances, which help bring this unsettling chapter of American history to the screen.

Inspired by true events, “By Any Means” is set in 1960s Mississippi, where a wave of brutal killings targeting civil rights leaders prompts the FBI to launch an investigation. Young agent Wayne Strider (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) is assigned to uncover those responsible, but promptly encounters resistance as local authorities appear reluctant to help. With witnesses too frightened to come forward and key suspects seemingly protected, Strider is forced into an unlikely partnership with notorious New York Mafia hitman Greg Scarpa (Mark Wahlberg). As the pair travel across Mississippi gathering information and confronting suspected killers, their vastly different methods create a volatile working relationship.

Premieres December 3 on Paramount+.

Industry observers note that taylor Sheridan is expanding the “Tulsa King” universe with “Frisco King,” a crime comedy-drama led by Samuel L. Jackson. The series follows Jackson’s character after his introduction in a two-episode arc during “Tulsa King” season 3, giving fans another chance to enjoy his wonderfully dry humor and effortless screen presence. Sylvester Stallone is also set to make a crossover appearance, adding another familiar face to the mix. Sheridan serves as creator, showrunner and sole writer across all eight episodes.

Industry observers note that “Frisco King” follows Russell Lee Washington Jr. (Samuel L. Jackson), a seasoned New Orleans gangster who relocates to Frisco, Texas, looking to establish a new criminal operation. After discovering a thriving underground network of hustlers operating beneath the town’s respectable suburban exterior, Lee begins recruiting a team to help expand his business. His new associates include Teddy (Asa Germann), an ambitious college dropout who becomes his protégé, and Keith (Kai Caster), a local hotel valet who joins his operation. Alongside two local cheerleaders, Lee turns small-time schemes into increasingly lucrative ventures.

Premieres December 18 on Paramount+.

Industry observers note that another series worth adding to your watchlist is “The Day,” a British crime thriller adapted from the 2018 Belgian series. The bank heist setup is intriguing enough, but it’s interesting how the story unfolds from two different perspectives, shifting between the police negotiating outside and the people trapped inside the bank. Each episode reveals more about what happened, gradually changing how you view earlier events. The series also boasts a strong cast, including Minnie Driver, making it a good choice if you’re after a gripping crime drama with a slightly different storytelling approach.

The series centers around a bank robbery that takes an unexpected turn when police arrive in the middle of the heist, prompting the criminals to barricade themselves inside with several hostages. Minnie Driver stars as Sylvia “Vox” Voxley, a hostage negotiator tasked with bringing the situation under control before anyone gets hurt. However, as the siege unfolds, the story rewinds to revisit the events from inside the bank, revealing the perspectives of the robbers and their captives. Across eight episodes, the series switches between the police operation and the unfolding hostage crisis.

Premieres December 31 on Paramount+.

It’s a Thanksgiving Day tradition to gather the family around the TV to watch the best athletes in America contend for glory — we’re, of course, referring to the dogs of the National Dog Show, which sees two hours of canine competition across seven groups.

In a recent development, the National Dog Show has historically followed the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. This year will look a little different, as the Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed to Saturday, Nov. 28 due to severe weather. This marks the first time the parade has ever been postponed, although it was cancelled for several years during World War II. The National Dog Show, which was pre-taped earlier this month at the Greater Philadelphia Expo Center, is still scheduled to air as planned.

The show will air at noon, local time, on NBC and will be preceded by a replay of last year’s parade. Last year’s Best in Show was Soleil, a Belgian sheepdog, who is looking to defend her title this year. The dog breeds are split into seven groups: herding, hound, non-sporting, sporting, terrier, toy, and working.

The competition is presented by the Kennel Club of Philadelphia and sponsored by Purina, and the broadcast will be hosted by John O’Hurley and David Frei, who are returning for their 25th year.

If you’re looking to watch the National Dog Show, you can catch it on NBC. If you don’t have cable or an antenna, you can stream it by subscribing to Peacock, or by getting a free trial to a live-TV streaming service like DirecTV or Fubo. Here are a few options.

In a recent development, direcTV is one of the best live-TV streaming services thanks to its broad selection. You can get NBC a variety of packages, all of which come with a five-day trial.

Sources indicate that fubo carries NBC in both of its tiers and is a particularly popular streaming service with sports fans. Like DirecTV, you can get a five-day free trial. You also get a discount on the first month after the trial.

Hulu + Live TV has a shorter three-day free trial, and it includes NBC in its main plan. The service costs $99.99 a month once the trial ends.

11 of the Best Thanksgiving TV Episodes Ever

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1415 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s the Thanksgiving season, which means the turkey is in the oven, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade is on the screen, the pies are cooling on the countertop, and that box of Christmas lights you wadded up into a ball last year is waiting for you just around the corner.
  • Sources indicate that while the holiday season mainly involves eating your bodyweight in dishes made primarily of butter, it’s also about giving thanks.
  • From tense discussions about family fortunes and hijinks-heavy parent traps to just so many extra turkeys, here are 11 of the best Thanksgiving-themed episodes of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s the Thanksgiving season, which means the turkey is in the oven, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade is on the screen, the pies are cooling on the countertop, and that box of Christmas lights you wadded up into a ball last year is waiting for you just around the corner.

Sources indicate that while the holiday season mainly involves eating your bodyweight in dishes made primarily of butter, it’s also about giving thanks. And what better way to revel in the nostalgia of family gatherings than rewatching some of the most memorable Thanksgiving tables to ever grace television screens?

From tense discussions about family fortunes and hijinks-heavy parent traps to just so many extra turkeys, here are 11 of the best Thanksgiving-themed episodes of TV.

According to recent reports, throughout Upcoming Girl’s seven seasons, the gang share multiple Thanksgiving dinners — almost all of which immediately devolve into chaos. But there’s something infinitely rewatchable about “Parents,” where Jessica Day (Zoey Deschanel) attempts to get her divorced parents back together over the pumpkin pie. It’s a masterclass of character work from the late Rob Reiner and Jamie Lee Curtis  — who play Jess’s parents — and Curtis’ attempt to seduce Jessica’s crush Nick (Jake Johnson) with a turkey baster can’t be touched.

It has been revealed that sometimes life is good as a teenage Upper East Side socialite destined for Yale and the sweet life. And then sometimes, you’re Blair Waldorf (Leighton Meester) and you spend all day trying to perfect your family’s traditional pumpkin pie only for your father to bail on the dinner he promised he was coming to. At least your best friend is having a good time. Except, oh wait — all the way in Dumbo, Serena van der Woodsen (Blake Lively) finds out that her mother and her new boyfriend’s dad have spent decades pining after each other. With its sepia-toned flashbacks and classic 2000s pop hits, “Blair Waldorf Must Pie” defines the aesthetic of Gossip Girl and sets up Meester for a career-defining exercise in fleeting emotional openness.

According to recent reports, thanksgiving is famously a holiday that’s celebrated by overeating. But Gilmore Girls takes it to a hysterical level in “A Deep-Fried Korean Thanksgiving.” Lorelai (Lauren Graham) and Rory (Alexis Bledel) cherish the amount of friendship and love in their life. But when all of their friends want them to attend separate Thanksgiving dinners, they choose the worst of all the options and decide to attend all of them rather than let anyone down. The side-plot of Lane (Keiko Agena) and Dave Rygalski’s (Adam Brody) budding love and first kiss is a heartwarming addition to the madcap food marathon, which pushes the titular girls’ stomachs and secrets to the limit.

In a recent development, this Grey’s Anatomy Thanksgiving episode shows everyone’s favorite medical residents pushed to their breaking points when their social lives crash into their professional goals. Yes, it’s especially memorable to watch the often-bullied George O’Malley (T.R. Knight) finally find common ground with his camo-wearing, gun toting family. But the crux of this episode is the gastronomic stylings of Dr. Burke (Isaiah Washington) and Izzie Stevens (Katherine Heigl), who treat their prepped kitchen like an O.R. — turning their Thanksgiving feast into a lesson in surgery.

Sources indicate that family means quality time. It also means knowing when not to have faith in your relatives. When Phil (Ty Burrell) takes over turkey duty for Thanksgiving, his wife Claire (Julie Bowen) makes a secret backup. But when an electric problem forces them to decamp to her father’s house, Jay (Ed O’Neill) and Gloria (Sofia Vergara) have to stay in their rooms or admit to the extended crew that they faked leaving on a  Thanksgiving cruise to avoid the drama of the holidays. It’s practically a carnival game with turkeys moving in and out of the oven, capped off with some truly comical voice work from cooking legend Nigella Lawson.

According to recent reports, it might feel a bit blasphemous to not include the Bobs Burger episode that gave us Linda Belcher’s famous Thanksgiving-themed melody “Pass the cranberry sauce.” But in “Turkey In a Can,” Bob’s Burgers leaves the set dressing behind and tackles the real stressor behind Thanksgiving: sexual awakening. When Bob (H. Jon Benjamin) wakes up before Thanksgiving to find his brining turkey in the toilet, he has to keep making daily trips to the butcher to replace it. The butcher (Tuc Watkins) naturally thinks Bob is flirting — although he’s not usually into “sloppy bears,” as he puts it — but the return visits wear him down until Bob has to reject his advances. Not because he’s married, but because he’s “mostly straight.”.

Industry observers note that while press secretary CJ Cregg (Allison Janney) has to choose which of the turkeys wins a presidential pardon, President Josiah Bartlett (Martin Sheen) has to make an infinitely harder choice — deciding whether a boat of Chinese immigrants seeking religious refugee status will be allowed to stay in the country. Aaron Sorkin is a man of many words, but sometimes he pulls off an episodic feat that feels virtually impossible to emotionally recreate. It’s no wonder that “Shibboleth” — and its titular discussion about faith — remains one of the most beloved episodes in the entire series.

Industry observers note that you think your Thanksgiving dinner table gets a little tense? At least you’re not Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), who’s trying to figure out how to keep his affair a secret, teach his teenager not to take ecstasy, and figure out whether or not to kill one of his henchmen in the same night — all while trying to ignore his sister’s fresh born-again boyfriend. Through its six seasons, The Sopranos takes care to show the immediate cost and unexpected struggles of running a mob empire — leaning heavy on moments of tense expecation. But “He Is Risen” takes the already comical moments in the mob series and slams them onto one crowded dinner table.

According to recent reports, yes, it’s a truth universally acknowledged that Ryan Murphy’s hit high school drama Glee completely jumped the shark once its main characters graduated and had to leave the halls of their beloved William McKinley High School. But the series’ relocation from Lima, Ohio to the streets of Latest York made even more magical celebrity run-ins become slightly more plausible. It’s a true gift that keeps on giving to be able to watch Sarah Jessica Parker, playing a Vogue editor, attend Rachel Berry and Kurt Hummel’s Bushwick-loft Thanksgiving. And once you watch her perform a mashup of “Let’s Have A Kiki / Turkey Lurkey Time,” this episode will become an annual must-watch.

Whenever you turn on an episode of Succession, you can pretty much be assured that Kendall Roy (Jeremy Strong) is having a no good, terrible, very bad day. But Succession’s Thanksgiving episode “I Went To The Market” does more than place Kendall’s long-suffering air front and center. It uses the Thanksgiving holiday to prove just how unsuited the entire family is being normal. While Kendall preparing a vote of no-confidence is the crux of the episode, much of the humor coalesces around Cousin Greg (Nicholas Braun)’s trip driving his grandfather Ewan (James Cromwell) — Logan’s brother — down from Canada. In addition to the signature Tom Wambsgans quips — “Canada, with the healthcare and the ennui?” — Tom (Matthew Macfadyen) has to figure out his prenup with Shiv and how to destroy records of the Brightstar Cruise Lines crimes at the same time. It’s classic Succession — no one gets turkey before a little corporate espionage.

I don’t care if there’s an episode where Monica (Courtney Cox) actually puts a turkey on her head — the one  with Brad Pitt as a secret guest star remains an ideal Friends scenario. In “The One with the Rumor,” Pitt stars as Will Colbert, Monica’s high school friend who indicates up to Thanksgiving unrecognizable after losing over 150 pounds. “It’s no fat, no sugar, no dairy,” Pitt states, handing Monica a pie. “It’s no good, throw it out.” His arrival was a surprise to the live studio audience, who shriek in delight at his appearance. (Pitt was married to Friends cast member Jennifer Aniston at the time.) Watching the cast fight over the barbs they traded in high school means a flurry of jokes, but it’s the delighted screams and cheers behind the camera that sell this episode.

#200176. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (715 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the biggest glitch with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat.
  • MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.
  • Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the biggest glitch with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker claims it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

Industry observers note that the MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker claims that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

According to recent reports, there’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also swiftly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

It has been revealed that qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I mentioned in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

Black Friday scammers are targeting iPhones — turn on these iOS settings before you shop

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between back to back flash sales, urgent delivery updates, and constant order confirmations, Black Friday is prime hunting season for scammers trying to blend into a crowded inbox.
  • Taking two minutes to adjust a handful of built-in iOS protections puts an immediate barrier between your personal data and the most common holiday checkout traps, without slowing down your shopping.
  • If your iPhone is running iOS 27, Apple’s newer anti-scam safeguard helps flag suspicious activity before money or account access changes hands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between back to back flash sales, urgent delivery updates, and constant order confirmations, Black Friday is prime hunting season for scammers trying to blend into a crowded inbox. Even cautious iPhone owners can get caught off guard when a fake package alert or spoofed bank warning lands right alongside real receipts.

Taking two minutes to adjust a handful of built-in iOS protections puts an immediate barrier between your personal data and the most common holiday checkout traps, without slowing down your shopping.

If your iPhone is running iOS 27, Apple’s newer anti-scam safeguard helps flag suspicious activity before money or account access changes hands. Open Settings, Privacy & Security, Impersonation Risk Detection and turn on sharing with app developers.

When enabled, supported banking and shopping apps can receive risk signals (categorized as unknown, medium, or high) to pause or re-verify sensitive actions like payments, transfers, or password changes if someone is trying to coach you through a scam over the phone.

Industry observers note that scammers rely heavily on rapid-fire cold calls pretending to be fraud departments or tech support. Go to Settings, Accessibility, Audio & Visual, Call Audio Routing and double-check that Auto-Answer Calls is toggled off. Keeping it disabled ensures your iPhone will not accidentally pick up an incoming spam call on its own while connected to AirPods, headphones, or your car’s Bluetooth.

Fake courier texts claiming a missed delivery or unpaid customs fee surge during Black Friday weekend. Head to Settings, Apps, Messages, then scroll down to the Unknown Senders section, and toggle on both Screen Unknown Senders and Filter Spam.

Recent findings suggest that this sweeps suspicious texts out of your main inbox automatically. If you still want alerts for legitimate automated messages, such as two-factor login codes or time-sensitive delivery updates, tap Allow Notifications underneath and customize which categories can still buzz your screen.

The actor could face ⁠15-20 years in jail if he ⁠is convicted.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, a lawyer for Arnould, described the ruling as a relief. “She has been waiting for this moment for a long time,” Durrieu ​Diebolt told Reuters. “She is fully ​prepared for it.”.

Earlier this month, Depardieu dropped his appeal of a recent sexual-assault verdict and admitted to groping two women on a movie set in 2021. Depardieu’s appeal trial was scheduled to begin on Nov. 16 in Paris, but however his lawyer released a statement announcing the actor’s decision instead. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5.
  • Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers.
  • In a recent development, you still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a fresh, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

In a recent development, you still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

According to recent reports, if you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

According to recent reports, there are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a fresh console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:.

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

Recent findings suggest that by far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.
