💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift.
  • In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem.
  • The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up….

In a recent development, the Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big enhancement last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people latest to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

According to recent reports, the Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a significant update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-fresh Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the organization conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”.

Recent findings suggest that with the latest system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

In a recent development, as I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The fresh sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people upcoming to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

#200167. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • It has been revealed that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

In a recent development, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

It has been revealed that the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn swiftly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

According to recent reports, miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Industry observers note that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

According to recent reports, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly demonstrates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

According to recent reports, to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most vital processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

According to recent reports, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It has been revealed that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Sources indicate that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller indicates. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

In a recent development, the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

It has been revealed that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller claims with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

Sources indicate that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

Sources indicate that as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

It has been revealed that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Sources indicate that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Sources indicate that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

In a recent development, “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller indicates with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

It has been revealed that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” claims Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

Industry observers note that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller claims. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that “What are you?
  • In a recent development, over the next few months, Ross will attempt to strike a rather unique balance as coach and touring artist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is arguably no better day for football — watching it or playing it — than the autumnal crispness of Thanksgiving. But on this particular late summer afternoon, despite triple-digit temperatures and the Oklahoma sun making it feel even hotter, football is the sweat-drenched task at hand: Coach Kyle Ross is putting me through practice. It’s not lost on either of us that Ross’s primary job is coaching high-energy junior-high athletes in the state’s flagship football program, at Bixby, and I’m an out-of-shape journalist in his late 40s. If I finish Ross’s drills upright and healthy, we’ll declare it a success.

Industry observers note that “What are you? Three-for-three or four-for-four catching passes here?” Ross — who is also the founder and frontman of the band Keyland — asks me. My football career ended in high school, 30 years ago, but I was a slot receiver with a reputation for catching anything thrown my way. What would my parents say if I started dropping passes now? “I will throw my body on this turf to not miss a pass,” I promise him.

In a recent development, over the next few months, Ross will attempt to strike a rather unique balance as coach and touring artist. He’ll headline and sell out the Mercury Lounge in Tulsa, 30 minutes north of Bixby, open an East Coast run for Morgan Wade, and announce a series of 2027 dates supporting Kaitlin Butts. And while he’s ostensibly promoting Knuckle Sandwich, Keyland’s third studio album, Ross will always have football season in the back of his mind.

Industry observers note that “I haven’t found anything better to do,” Ross claims of why he continues to coach. “Except for maybe, get paid to play guitar and drink beer.”.

Few pastimes are as all-encompassing in Oklahoma as football. Its two largest college programs — Oklahoma and Oklahoma State — play their home games in modern stadiums to sold-out crowds on most Saturdays in the fall, but it’s the high-school version of the sport that unites the state. Students, fans, and parents fill stadiums in the state’s urban cores and rural farm towns every Friday night, and for the past decade, no program has dominated this landscape like Bixby’s. The varsity Spartans are eight-time defending champions in Oklahoma’s largest class and this season were ranked No. 1 again by the state’s largest media outlet. This is Ross’s program. He’s an assistant coach for Bixby’s eighth-grade team and a junior-high English teacher. He grew up in rural Missouri, playing football through high school. Shortly after graduating college, Ross befriended Tyler Schneider — Bixby’s longtime offensive coordinator. The two hit it off, and within weeks, Ross joined the Spartan’s staff. Seven years later, Ross is throwing passes to me on the same turf that those Spartans play their home games. We’re here to talk about music, but I am here to experience what it’s like being one of Ross’s players.

Sources indicate that “Let’s go!” he shouts as I haul in another pass. “And he scores!”.

It has been revealed that as it happens, that particular end zone is where I scored my last touchdown as a player. Before Bixby became the state’s juggernaut program, it was a mid-sized school in the same conference as my hometown team, the Okmulgee Bulldogs.

When he’s playing as Keyland — Ross uses the moniker interchangeably for his solo and full-band reveals, named for a duck club he and his father used to hunt near his Chillicothe, Missouri, hometown — he wears an infectious smile that’s integral to his show. He describes the irreverent Knuckle Sandwich, which Keyland recorded at the Sonic Ranch studio outside of El Paso, as a product of pals hanging around for several days and finding music at the end of it. Related Content Jason Scott and the High Heat Are the Cool, If Raunchy, Band Americana Music Needs Honky-Tonk Woman: Kaitlin Butts Is As Ambitious As She Wants to Be You’ve Been Streaming ‘Broken Window Serenade.’ This Is the Texas Band Who Wrote It Wade Bowen Is Texas Music.

“This album is about taking what you do seriously, but not taking yourself seriously,” Ross states. “That kind of embodies the whole creative process in recording it. It’s more of a hang than anything, and we get music at the end of it.”.

Industry observers note that it’s a microcosm for his entire music career. He had a guitar growing up, but played it sparingly. It was not until he was in college and caught a Chris Stapleton gig that he decided to give music a try. “I fell in love with Chris Stapleton, and that was the entry way to the long rabbit hole I fell into,” he claims.

Landing a full-time job right in the heart of Tulsa’s music community was a bout of good fortune. Ross befriended Brandon Clark, frontman of the Red Dirt outfit BC & the Big Rig and highly respected in Red Dirt circles. Clark has a weekly gig at Mercury Lounge, and in 2022, he suggested that Keyland get booked at the bar.

Industry observers note that keyland’s first Mercury Lounge show was opening for the Big Rig. Shortly afterward, venue general manager Ashley Kirkley booked Keyland as a headliner. The show sold out, and Keyland have been a regular since.

Industry observers note that “Keyland is a great band, no doubt, but the energy and charisma that emanates from Kyle is palpable at every show,” Kirkley says. “Beyond being an incredible performer with a distinctive voice that is unlike anything I’ve heard, he is also one of the most down to earth, kindest people I have ever met. Kyle is always striving for greatness in everything he does. He’s an incredible human, and we are incredibly lucky to have him as a part of our music family.”.

In a recent development, keyland have since gone on to, at least, regional notoriety. Ross has been booked multiple times at nearby Cain’s Ballroom, playing alongside the likes of Johnny Mullenax and opening a sold-out show for Josh Abbott earlier this year.

“Everyone’s at different levels of what they’re doing,” Ross says of the Tulsa music community. “I have friends who have sold out a place like Cain’s. I’m friends with people who are doing house demonstrates for ten people. It almost seems like everyone has a very similar mindset of, ‘We’re almost there.’”.

Sources indicate that ross knows better than anyone that Keyland is growing at a fast clip. He is likely to come to a crossroads between coaching and making music before too many more gigs or summer practices pass. But until then, he’s happy to pull double duty. And even at Bixby, where the focus is annually on another state championship, he has found support. He had a fan from the start in Schneider, but he’s brought most of the Spartans’ coaching staff onto his bandwagon — and even a few players.

According to recent reports, “There’s a huge Venn diagram of coaches’ interests outside of football, and one of them is music,” Ross says. “All the coaches are super supportive. We have over 20 coaches, and a huge number of them have been to more than one concert. It’s just a community-oriented place to work. The kids, as they get older, they start to appreciate it.”.

And on that note, practice is over. Ross’s actual players are starting to trickle in to Bixby’s behemoth of a training facility. Ross gives me a Bixby Spartans shirt for surviving his drills. Recent findings suggest that anthropic is launching a upcoming tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”.

Recent findings suggest that claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic states. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”.

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

In a recent development, mowing the lawn is one of those homeowner chores that never gets less annoying—more so if you have a sizeable lawn. Keeping the grass in check can take up most of your weekend, but like a robot vacuum taking the brunt of your housework duties, a robotic lawn mower can do the yardwork for you.

Sources indicate that right now, MAMMOTION is offering substantial Black Friday savings on its LUBA lineup of lawn mowers, bringing the LUBA mini 2 AWD 1500H down to $1,599, from $1,999. Meanwhile, the more powerful LUBA 3 AWD 3000 is down to $1,999 from its usual $2,799. Both deals include a free mower wash stand, valued at $79. That’s up to $800 of combined savings, and the offers run through Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

If you’re picking between the two lawn mowers, your choice largely depends on the size of the area you’re mowing. The LUBA mini 2 AWD 1500H is designed for small and medium-sized yards, with a 360-degree LiDAR navigation system to map out your lawn and identify obstacles. The all-wheel-drive system can tackle slopes of up to 80%, and the side-mounted cutting disc helps it get closer to walls, fences, and flower beds.

According to recent reports, for larger properties, the LUBA 3 AWD 3000 is a solid fit. This lawn mower includes the same 360-degree LiDAR navigation system, but pairs it with 4G-based Network RTK functionality and AI vision, so the mower stay on course without boundary wires or a separate antenna. It can also handle slopes as steep as 80%, and its 15.7-inch cutting width and two cutting discs can handle up to 5,400 square feet per hour. The AI vision system allows it to recognise and avoid 300 different types of obstacles, including toys and pets.

Both mowers are designed to remove much of the manual work associated with yard maintenance. Once configured, these mowers can manage multiple mowing zones, customize schedules, and varied cutting heights.

Priced at $1,599, the LUBA mini 2 is a fairly substantial investment, but the $400 Black Friday discount and free wash stand make it a bit easier to justify. Similarly, the LUBA 3 gets a more significant $800 savings, plus the wash stand. If you’ve been considering a robotic lawn mower to bring some automation to the outdoors, these Black Friday offers are worth a look.

#200159. All the ‘GTA’ Games Ever, Ranked

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3266 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollingstone ↗ Open Full Page

All the ‘GTA’ Games Ever, Ranked

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that unless you’ve been locked in a bank vault somewhere for the last 30 years, there’s a good chance that you’ve heard of Grand Theft Auto.
  • But more so than the money, GTA’s influence on gaming and culture at large is its true legacy.
  • Sources indicate that outside of the industry sphere, GTA became a touchstone for gaming as a concept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that unless you’ve been locked in a bank vault somewhere for the last 30 years, there’s a good chance that you’ve heard of Grand Theft Auto. Originally introduced for PC and PlayStation in 1997, the series began as a solid commercial success for fans of edgy humor and shooters, before becoming a pop culture phenomenon in the early 2000s. Today, it’s one of the most recognizable entertainment properties on Earth, transcending the boundaries of just gaming — with its latest iteration, GTA VI, arriving this year with the highest grossing media launch ever. Day one sales of GTA VI generated over $3.79 billion, more than any other game or movie, amounting to the GDP of a small nation.

But more so than the money, GTA’s influence on gaming and culture at large is its true legacy. The open-world crime saga has informed the way video games are developed; its cinematic tone nailed an old Hollywood flavor that earlier games could only vaguely emulate; the freedom of choice in how to play inspired imitators of all kinds, from kid-friendly fare to direct copycats chasing the violent gangster gameplay.

Sources indicate that outside of the industry sphere, GTA became a touchstone for gaming as a concept. Think of any movie or show where characters are playing video games; it’s very likely the visual depiction will be a crudely rendered clone of GTA. A target of endless pearlclutching, politicians and advocates on both sides of the aisle have paraded the name as a leading cause of societal decay. To some, it’s a hedonistic simulacrum of sex and violence, encouraging players to indulge their darkest impulses.

And, sure, it’s a series where you can assault sex workers and commit mass shootings, but those options bely the point of Grand Theft Auto as a whole. At their best, the games serve as an intricately written parody of American culture — the greed, hypocrisy, and often downright idiocy that the country wears so proudly. In GTA, the American Dream is something to be gripped by force, and is delivered to audiences through caricature. It takes all the stories, media, and norms we love and reflects them back as satire. GTA doesn’t glorify crime, people do. It’s just laughing at us along the way.

To that end, not every GTA is so successful. The early top-down entries served more as arcade-style run-and-gunners that did little to admonish players to think beyond wanton destruction. But as technology evolved and storytelling devices matured, GTA began to better embody its role as Mean Streets meets South Park, telling exaggerated tales of criminality gone wrong to make audiences flinch — at least momentarily, before plotting their next heist.

It has been revealed that in honor of GTA VI’s long-awaited release, Rolling Stone is ranking every Grand Theft Auto, from their humble Nineties-era origins to the modern blockbusters, both main games and expansions. Here’s every one, from worst to best.

According to recent reports, although the first two games in the series made appearances on the Game Boy Color, Grand Theft Auto Advance was the first original entry specifically developed for a Nintendo device. Blending the top-down overhead perspective of the OG installments with the mission structure of then-ubiquitous 3D versions, GTA Advance bridges the series’ oft-forgotten older design with more accessible gameplay.

Sources indicate that as a prequel to 2001’s GTA III, players control a low-rent criminal named Mike whose dream of leaving Liberty City behind is blown to shreds by the mafia. Storywise, the plot comes through mostly via text and isn’t much to cling to. The handheld hardware of the Game Boy Advance doesn’t allow for much graphical fidelity, resulting in a game that looks worse than even the first PC entry, but is still commendable as a pocket-friendly way to play GTA.

According to recent reports, to capitalize on the success of the original game, two expansions were green-lit as interim teasers before 1999’s full-fledged sequel. Grand Theft Auto: London 1969 released earlier that year as a standalone purchase, with 1961 following suit as a free download. Neither entry was groundbreaking, mostly recycling the gameplay and visuals of the base game with a Swingin’ Sixties finish. The duology is mostly fascinating for being the only GTA games set in a real city rather than fictional versions of American locales. The setting did result in one major innovation, however, with licensed music introduced to the franchise for the in-game radio stations — a feature that would become an essential part of GTA’s appeal moving forward.

Looking back, it’s hard to imagine how a game as simple as the original Grand Theft Auto kickstarted a media dynasty. Developed by Scottish studio DMA Design (now Rockstar North), the initial concept began as a simple cops and robbers sim called Race ‘n’ Chase, before being overhauled to focus on the more open-ended crime-oriented mission structure. Players choose from an assortment of unnamed protagonists to control, and must complete six linear levels spread across three cities (Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City), accruing a set number of points to progress.

Although seemingly basic in its top-down design, with a world composed mostly of tiny dot-like people and a handful of vehicle options, the first GTA built the foundation for everything else to come. Its six levels each serve as small sandboxes where players can choose to score cash as they see fit, and each city would later be fleshed out as fully realized urban sprawls in the 3D games. Like any of the series’ main characters, this freshman outing represents a humble start with great aspirations.

Sources indicate that while the first batch of Game Boy Color and Advance releases proved that the series’ formula could be replicated for handheld with a few concessions, Liberty City Stories took things a step further — bringing a fully 3D GTA to the PlayStation Portable. Like GTA Advance, this all-fresh entry serves as a prequel to GTA III, albeit much more faithfully rendered, with graphics matching the home console version and even fully recorded voice acting for its cinematic cut scenes. In fact, it’s superior in some ways, incorporating gameplay features like changeable clothing and more intuitive camera controls. Once ported to the PlayStation 2, the game’s cracks began to show slightly; it’s a mostly inessential side quest for those who want more GTA III. But, in its initial portable incarnation, Liberty City Stories is a technical marvel.

Industry observers note that the second spinoff developed for PlayStation Portable, Vice City Stories is yet another shining example of the impressive capabilities of Sony’s first foray into the handheld market. A prequel to 2002’s Vice City, it carries over the Eighties setting and includes an impressive voice cast for what’s essentially a mobile game, including Gary Busey, Miami Vice star Philip Michael Thomas, and even Phil Collins as himself.

Unlike its PSP predecessor, Vice City Stories does more than just replicate the console experience on-the-go, introducing some very ambitious fresh mechanics to the experience. The most prominent is the concept of empire building, where players must topple local local gang-affiliated businesses, then usurp control to create a network of private income sources, from brothels to protection rackets. Also like the previous game, Vice City Stories features a six-person multiplayer mode, although that feature was removed for the later PlayStation 2 rerelease.

While GTA as a series frequently pivots between settings and perspectives, Chinatown Wars marks some of the biggest departures for the franchise’s look and gameplay overall. The handheld game blends the top-down view of the early titles with a new cel-shaded aesthetic with thick character and environmental outlines reminiscent of a comic book. Initially designed for the dual-screen Nintendo DS, its gameplay features numerous touchscreen-based minigames — although both these controls and the stylized visuals were swapped out for the later PSP release.

Recent findings suggest that but the most notable change in Chinatown Wars is a greater emphasis on drug-dealing, something that was controversial at release. As a Triad member, players can sell heroin, ecstasy, weed, cocaine and more — as well as strategize around different market conditions and geographical supply. It’s a murky system that goes deeper than most games in the series, which mostly ask the user to smuggle narcotics rather than peddle them directly.

Sources indicate that at launch, GTA 2 was met with a mixed reception, mostly for failing to meaningfully innovate beyond the first game’s premise and design. But that’s not entirely true. The 1997 original did well to introduce the basics of open-ended mission structure and player choice, but its sequel perfected the formula for the pseudo-2D era.

Set in a fictional retro-futuristic city called Anywhere, U.S.A., GTA 2 sees players once again controlling a itty bitty protagonist as they conduct crime in a sequence of missions to progress through each level. This time, the setting is one large city divided by districts, and features rival gangs to work for, each at odds with each other. Balancing favor between the syndicates is key, and an increased level of environmental interactivity can lead to gang members engaging in their own immersive firefights with the police and each other. GTA 2 isn’t quite the quantum leap forward that its successor would be, but it’s a delightful piece of retro gaming nostalgia whose DNA can be seen in later indie games like Hotline Miami (2012).

Before the turn of the millennium, the GTA series had been a modest success, selling millions of units on PC and PlayStation, but it hadn’t quite hit the zeitgeist. GTA III would be the beginning of the dominant cultural force we know today. Rebooting the series’ narrative into a upcoming continuity moving forward, it once again drops players into the New York-inspired setting of Liberty City — now rendered in full 3D — for an exponentially more cinematic experience.

For gamers, GTA III is a foundational text, popularizing many design choices and mechanics today’s player take for granted. Its urban open-world feels lived in, peppered with cars and pedestrians, each on their own loop that can be upended. Combat and gunplay, while simplistic by modern standards, are deeper than ever before thanks to the 3D leap; the ability to simultaneously drive a car and aim over-the-shoulder for a drive-by was astounding at the time. Most importantly, the first entry of this new era allowed Rockstar to fully realize the cinematic scope of what Grand Theft Auto always wanted to be. With elaborate cut scenes and voice acting from stars Frank Vincent, Debi Mazar, and Kyle MacLachlan, GTA III pioneered the blurring of lines between games and cinema. It’s basically gaming’s Mean Streets, a New Hollywood crime caper from which generations of developers would borrow from moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that much like the original game, 2008’s GTA IV received a duology of expansions that built on the base game’s foundation. But unlike the London content, The Lost and the Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony substantially add to the narrative and mechanics of their progenitor beyond being simple reskins.

Sources indicate that each expansion follows characters whose stories overlap with the main plot of GTA IV: biker Johnny Klebitz in the TLATD and bodyguard Luis Fernando Lopez in TBOGT. While both play similarly, each has distinct features beyond the base game. Johnny’s motorcycle club plays a huge role in his content, allowing players to call in the gang for backup when things get hairy. Luis’ gameplay isn’t notably different, but the story in his expansion is one of the very best in the series, celebrated at the time for its depiction of LGBTQ characters.

Sources indicate that there was a time when game development was a much speedier process, with studios rapidly churning out quality sequels near annually. Rockstar themselves had a generational run from 2001 to 2004, dominating the conversation with the trifecta of GTA III, Vice City, and San Andreas. Even more impressive is how each game substantially improved on its predecessor despite wildly shifting apart in setting and tone.

According to recent reports, vice City falls squarely in the middle of the pack, transposing GTA III’s groundbreaking design into a Miami Vice and Scarface-inspired Eighties crime caper, complete with a lead character voiced by actor Ray Liotta. Control-wise, it’s not a huge leap forward; players still roam an open world hopping between main missions, side quests, and mini-games. What elevates Vice City is its pitch perfect take on Eighties Miami, depicting a greasy city soaked in neon, all set to one of the greatest video game soundtracks of all time.

Until very recently, GTA V was the series’ most ambitious entry to date. For many, it’s the definitive Grand Theft Auto experience — if only by default. The sole franchise entry in 13 years, GTA V was released for PlayStation 3, 4, and 5, selling a ludicrous 230 million copies over the course of its elongated lifespan.

Sources indicate that in many ways, GTA V plays like a greatest hits of the series’ many ideas and mechanics, while modernizing its gameplay just enough to feel like an improvement over IV. Set in the fictional state of San Andreas (although set in a different “universe” than the 2004 title of that name), the story follows three unique protagonists, all with conflicting personalities and motives. Players will bounce between bank robber Michael De Santa, gangster Franklin Clinton, and psychopathic gunrunner Trevor Philips; their interwoven narrative bringing a slightly meandering Tarantino vibe to the otherwise kinetic plot, heavily inspired by Michael Mann’s Heat. Fans would be right to argue that GTA V deserves the top spot based on popularity alone, but looking back on the actual gameplay, it did little to substantially innovate over its direct predecessor. In 2013, GTA V’s gameplay arrived feeling dated, but was bolstered significantly by its feeling of limitless freedom and well-executed campaign story.

In a recent development, although the series has many flavors, there’s a semblance of homogeny among the distinct crime syndicates throughout GTA. Regardless of the time period, there’s usually a depiction of the Italian mafia, Chinese Triads, maybe some Russians — with some depiction of Cuban and Haitian gangs cropping up in Vice City. 2004’s San Andreas broke served as a massive departure, centering on SoCal gang violence inspired by the Bloods and Crips.

In a recent development, while so much of the franchise’s inspiration seemingly comes from TV and movies (what better societal reflection, after all), San Andreas feels more informed by actual history, weaving in elements of real-life urban crises like the Nineties crack epidemic and the 1992 L.A. riots alongside storytelling lifted from films like John Singleton’s Boyz n the Hood. Outside of its unique setting and more impactful storytelling, one of San Andreas’ greatest contributions is an increased emphasis on the slice-of-life details and mini-games that shape the player character directly — something that is heavily prevalent in this year’s fresh entry, GTA VI.

Following a legendary run from 2001 to 2006, wherein five 3D GTA releases dominated home consoles and handhelds alike, the expectations for the next numbered entry in the franchise hit a fever pitch in 2008. Fortunately, GTA IV delivered the goods.

Sources indicate that resetting the table once again with a fresh vision of Liberty City, GTA IV traded in the sprawling map of San Andreas for a more densely packed and lively version of the series’ original locale. The story also eschewed any direct cinematic parallels to focus on a more original story leaning deeper into the satirical commentary of U.S. culture — specifically the American Dream. Unlike the thuggish mafioso types of games prior, GTA IV’s lead, Niko Bellic, is an ex-soldier and Eastern European immigrant, arriving in the states equally interested in revenge and a fresh start in the land of opportunity. Bringing in an outsider lends the game’s tone a sharper edge; this America is an alien place filled with unserious people.

Recent findings suggest that although its 2013 follow-up would offer better graphics and more features, GTA IV is essentially a perfected vision of what the 1997 original aimed to be, and stands less on the shoulders of other media to define its voice. This is the game that gave us Grand Theft Auto as we know it today.

Recent findings suggest that for all its many elements, the defining feature of Grand Theft Auto as an idea is the emphasis on player freedom. Go anywhere, do whatever you want — that’s the ultimate promise. Except, every GTA is bound by the needs of a linear narrative. There’s a story to tell, players are just a part of it. But what if the story was entirely your own?

GTA Online released as a 30-player online sandbox that emulated the mission structure of the base game while opening the door to infinite chaos. Rather than chasing down CPU-scripted non-playable characters, users are suddenly even squared against other humans who can react strategically (or erratically), turning the meta-gameplay of GTA to a upcoming level without the constraints of a campaign story. But storytelling is still key, and following the game’s PC launch in 2015, modders cracked open GTA Online’s world with limitless potential. Now, it’s a platform where online roleplay reigns supreme, a second-life simulator where people go about their daily routines under fictional personas.

In a recent development, on streaming platforms, content creators have turned GTA RP into everything from reality TV to serial killer soap operas. It’s transcended individual gameplay to become its own ever-present world of entertainment to control or passively watch. While GTA V has kept selling throughout console generations, it’s clear that GTA Online has been the lifeblood of the series in its interim time between installments, and racked up billions in revenue that’s funded the series’ next substantial phase.

There are certain moments in time when a game changes everything. Pong had families enraptured around their cathode ray TVs; Tetris locked people into their screens on-the-go decades before smart phones became the norm. As a series, Grand Theft Auto’s had its fair share of these moments. GTA III stunned gamers with its open world, and V made it feel like it was possible live within a movie.

According to recent reports, GTA VI might be the most incredible feat that Rockstar’s ever executed. From its opening moments, it’s instantly clear that there’s some insane technical alchemy going on. Its characters and environments are near photorealistic, and its world brimming with life. You can touch or do just about anything. In fact, players will spend their first few hours simply making coffee and painting their house.

Sources indicate that but beyond the flashy graphics and complex coding of NPC and environmental scripts, the most immediate difference in GTA VI is how mature it feels — and not in the adults-only content kind of way. Its dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, aren’t jade caricatures of criminals pulled from pop media, but instead richly humanized characters with hopes and dreams. Although the game has all the hallmarks of a Grand Theft Auto underworld story, every written beat and player action serves to inform how the relationship between its leads blossoms. Arriving in 2026 to an American culture that’s well beyond parody, Rockstar’s decision to ground its story in the perspective of genuine people elevates it beyond anything the franchise was ever intended to be. GTA VI perfectly encompasses all that excess that Grand Theft Auto should have, while adding in a soul we never knew it so desperately needed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the latest Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.
  • According to recent reports, the Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Offering support for iPhone and Android’s tracking networks, the latest Kodak SlideTag offers the neat added functionality over an AirTag of being able to show your photos and more on an E-Ink display.

According to recent reports, the Kodak SlideTag is inspired by classic 35mm slides from Kodak cameras, and is built by the same company, Reto, that launched a keychain digital camera inspired by old Kodak cameras too. The tracker’s E-Ink display is designed mainly to showcase your photos, with storage built-in for up to 12 photos, but also the ability to show lists and QR codes.

The SlideTag’s extra features are controlled by the Kodak Memory Link app, while tracking is handled in the Find My app on iPhone just like an AirTag (and the Find Hub app on Android phones).

Black Friday is bringing some substantial discounts on substantial-screen TVs this year, particularly for Costco members looking to upgrade without spending well over $1,000. From November 26 through November 30, the retailer is dropping the 100-inch Hisense QD7 to $999 from $1,799, an $800 discount, while the 85-inch Hisense U65 Pro will also cost $999, down from $1,299. Both models are Costco exclusives, and come with a three-year Allstate protection blueprint, bringing the total coverage to five years when combined with the manufacturer’s warranty.

According to recent reports, for anyone who puts sheer size first, the 100-inch QD7 offers an enormous viewing area for movies, sports, and gaming, with a 4K Hi-QLED display that uses Quantum Dot technology to produce richer, more vibrant colors. It's particularly appealing for a spacious living room or dedicated entertainment area, though you'll want to measure your wall and seating distance before committing to a screen this large. As for performance, the 85-inch QD7 offers a useful reference point, since CNET named it one of the best 85-inch TVs of 2026—and the two models share the same features apart from screen size.

The 85-inch U65 Pro, meanwhile, gives up 15 inches of screen space but adds Mini-LED backlighting with local dimming for better contrast and more controlled highlights, particularly in darker movie scenes. It also supports Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive, and a native 144Hz refresh rate, along with gaming features such as AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and variable refresh rate. That remarked, you don't have to go quite this big to get these features, as Costco is also discounting the 75-inch U65 Pro to $699 (from $899) and the 65-inch version to $529 (from $749). The latter is particularly worth considering, having earned an "outstanding" rating and an Editors' Choice award from PCMag.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the choice comes down to whether you'd prefer the extra screen space of the QD7 or the more advanced picture technology of the U65 Pro. Either way, these Black Friday discounts make a big-screen upgrade considerably more affordable for Costco members.

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with fresh customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube patch.

Industry observers note that in the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app released on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

In a recent development, android Authority spotted several latest app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta patch (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow owners to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

That stated, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

#200152. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2976 w)
