How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.
  • Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.
  • Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.

Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

Last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

In a recent development, the tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully introduced on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

In a recent development, this mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

In a recent development, “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” says Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”.

According to recent reports, phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

It has been revealed that scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

More than 10 years in the making, MMX launched on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a new rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA.

Industry observers note that MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes according to initiative, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images.

“It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” says Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

“If something doesn’t go according to plan, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” claims Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

It has been revealed that from that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot.

To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

The best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

In a recent development, during its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

It has been revealed that before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu notes, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA.

Sources indicate that it will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR.

“It will bounce probably several times,” says Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

A simulation highlights how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR.

Recent findings suggest that once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” indicates Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she claims. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”.

The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR.

The team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday claims.

Industry observers note that despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday notes Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy.

According to recent reports, idefix’s interactions with its latest home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”.

What Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel notes the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

In a recent development, once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

According to recent reports, the MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

The coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel says. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”.

Recent findings suggest that probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA.

The pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this issue and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu says.

Industry observers note that one of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

In a recent development, that possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA.

In a recent development, during the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

According to recent reports, once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA.

Finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

“We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel says. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

“MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu says. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

After the announcement yesterday that the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to weather, the event’s co-host Hoda Kotb stopped by Late Night to express her relief that it has been rescheduled for Saturday.

“The people who have been preparing this 100-year parade have been working tirelessly for a year-plus,” Kotb told host Seth Meyers. “The musical acts are incredible. So imagine spending all that time painting every little bit of every float, wondering if the float is going to fly away somewhere. So the good news is, to me, I’m relieved. Saturday is going to be amazing. Everybody’s still hanging out. We’re going to watch it anyway.”.

Recent findings suggest that she added, “It’s going to be literally out of this world. It’s amazing.”.

According to recent reports, weather experts have been warning U.S. residents about a rapidly approaching storm system making its way up the east coast, bringing with it high winds, heavy rains, and flood warnings. According to CNN, winds in Latest York City are expected to reach around 25 to 35 mph today — which would be dangerous for the parade’s famous floats and giant balloons.

“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s noted in a statement. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” Trending Stories Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Dead at 65 U2 Perform Dolly Parton's Final Recording During NFL Halftime Show Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys The Country Song About Losing Your Virginity That Became an Enduring Hit.

Sources indicate that this is the first time the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has been postponed because of inclimate weather. It was cancelled in 1942, 1943, and 1944 because the U.S. needed all excess helium and rubber for the World War II effort.

Kotb is set to co-host the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade alongside Savannah Guthrie and Al Roker. Grammy-nominated singer Raye is expected to open the parade with a holiday performance featuring her sisters, Amma and Absolutely; followed by floats and performances by Wyclef Jean, Smash Mouth, Natasha Bedingfield, Icona Pop, JoJo, Hunger Games star McKenna Grace, and Queen Latifah. No additional changes to the parade programming or lineup have been unveiled.

AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult.
  • Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.
  • In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then highlights how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

Industry observers note that apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently unveiled four upcoming features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the newly introduced design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

Sources indicate that iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently confirmed a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

Industry observers note that when shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a latest “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

It has been revealed that american Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a fresh “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

It has been revealed that this feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:.

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

It has been revealed that iPhone consumers with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

Industry observers note that this one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has revealed that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

Industry observers note that as Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes.
  • Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd).
  • Industry observers note that fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell.

Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd).

Industry observers note that fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Upgrade the kernel and reboot.

In a recent development, the NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes.

Recent findings suggest that commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE. It ships in Linux 3.16.

12 yearsEvery kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels.

Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report.

OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own.

CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes.

A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049.

Industry observers note that each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how substantial that cache is.

Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.

That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.

The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.

The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:.

The write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.

A replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.

A forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.

We refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.

We hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.

In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.

Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.

Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.

It has been revealed that tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.

On a distribution kernel, install the patch that lists CVE-2026-99362.

Recent findings suggest that then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.

Recent findings suggest that the attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:.

Sources indicate that we reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.

This 1996 classic comedy is the best movie to watch on Thanksgiving – and it's not even a Thanksgiving movie

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deck the halls with family drama … fa-la-la-la-awkward.
  • “The Birdcage” came out in 1996, yet 30 years later, it couldn’t be more relatable.
  • The Mike Nichols-directed film is certainly a product of its time, yet nearly a decade before “Brokeback Mountain,” it did far more for LGBTQ+ inclusivity than the infamous cowboy flick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deck the halls with family drama … fa-la-la-la-awkward. You don’t need Thanksgiving to start an argument at the dinner table, though it is the ultimate excuse to air every grievance you’ve suppressed since that doomed New Year’s resolution to "be more zen." (Spoiler alert: It didn’t stick.).

“The Birdcage” came out in 1996, yet 30 years later, it couldn’t be more relatable. Sure, it isn't marketed as a Thanksgiving movie, nor does it take place during the holiday. Still, the Robin Williams classic centers on a high-stakes family dinner showdown, serving sus soup — and plenty of political in-law drama — in bowls decked out with naked men. That kind of spice puts memaw’s pumpkin pie to shame.

The Mike Nichols-directed film is certainly a product of its time, yet nearly a decade before “Brokeback Mountain,” it did far more for LGBTQ+ inclusivity than the infamous cowboy flick.

The premise of “The Birdcage” sounds like an alpha-male podcaster’s worst nightmare: What happens when the not-so-demure daughter of a right-wing politician marries the son of a gay cabaret owner and his drag queen partner?

Sources indicate that there’s meeting the parents, and then there’s meeting your future son-in-law’s dad and his "wife" — who happens to be Albert in drag. Robin Williams anchors the film as doting dad Armand, while Nathan Lane plays Albert, his longtime partner. Their on-screen dynamic swings from heartfelt and wholesome to wildly theatrical without ever tipping into pure parody. Dan Futterman also brings an exasperated charm to Armand’s son, groom-to-be Val — no small feat for a guy asking his dad to step back into the closet to appease his future in-laws. Not cool, Val.

The "meet the parents" trope wasn't exactly fresh in ’96; the movie was adapted from Jean Poiret’s 1973 play, “La Cage aux Folles.” Yet Gene Hackman as ultra-conservative Senator Keeley, Dianne Wiest as his wife Louise, and Calista Flockhart as bride-to-be Barbara bring an unexpected edge to a rocky family dynamic (featuring some mild repression). Even Hank Azaria (Agador) and Christine Baranski (Katharine) steal every scene they’re in. The best part? Vocally homophobic Senator Keeley seems to have a bit of a thing for Albert in a wig. Who’s going to tell him?

Recent findings suggest that beneath the farce and political clash sits a relatable story about identity, loyalty and fighting for love that hits hard during Thanksgiving and the endless gauntlet of holiday obligations that follow. Even if you think the Goldmans are way too lenient on the Keeleys (yeah, hi), it’s always easier to watch someone else’s family meltdown than to survive your own.

You can certainly argue that “The Birdcage” isn’t perfect. It leans a little too heavily into femme stereotypes, traditional gender roles and "let's just agree to disagree" diplomacy at the queer characters' expense. Three decades on, though, it still feels like a movie that celebrates the queer community rather than treating us as the punchline, which is more than I can say for prestige dramas like “Brokeback Mountain” that double down on queer tragedy and shame. I usually champion queer stories led by creatives from the community, yet “The Birdcage” used its star-studded cast to pull mainstream audiences into an early, unapologetic celebration of queer joy.

What you take away from the movie ultimately depends on what you need. If it offers a blueprint for surviving clashing ideologies without a Thanksgiving panic attack, great. Personally, I see it as a reminder to love yourself loudly, regardless of who’s sitting across the table. Sister Sledge’s "We Are Family" plays throughout the film, but being family doesn't mean tolerating prejudice — it’s about championing a second, more vital bond: found family.

So, whether you put it on after dinner to scandalize Aunt Carol’s delicate sensibilities, or skip the family gathering altogether and protect your peace, “The Birdcage” is the exact antidote you need when you're dreading a family showdown before anyone even says grace.

Rent/buy "The Birdcage" to stream on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that I know the TV world can be super overwhelming — trust me, I’ve been there. So let’s do a quick rundown of the differences between the three “premium” panel types.

So an OLED has lots of mini diodes inside the panel that emit light individually. This means there’s no backlight, unlike older TVs. This means OLEDs are better for higher contrast, better blacks, better color, and smooth motion for gaming.

Sources indicate that QLEDs also use a light-emitting diode. Unlike OLED, a QLED panel has a backlight, which illuminates each diode individually. QLEDs are better for brighter rooms, as the panel itself tends to be brighter, but OLEDs can reach better contrast levels and color accuracy.

Mini-LED is something else entirely: it uses tiny LEDs (light-emitting diodes, like both QLED and OLED) — but thousands of them. That means each diode can pack a major color and brightness punch. Mini-LEDs can be brighter, blacker, and more colorful — all at once.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials.
  • The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….
  • Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” ….

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler claims, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

It has been revealed that there’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting organization to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

Sources indicate that the best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

#200125. The history of civilization is the history of wheat

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3854 w)

The history of civilization is the history of wheat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Asteriskmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving.
  • Together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides.
  • Industry observers note that the ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving. The original gods were forced to live in poverty. To solve this problem they created Ashnan, the goddess of grain, and Lahar, the god of sheep, and sent them to humans to cultivate their gifts.

Together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides. But the latest gods quarreled about which was greater. Enki, the god of wisdom, judged Ashnan the superior, reasoning that without grain there would be no bread, no beer, and, by extension, no cities and no Sumer.

Industry observers note that the ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people. Human consumption of wheat is older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel. In fact, some of the very earliest surviving examples of writing, which, like wheat, originate in the Middle East, aren’t epic poems or religious texts but administrative records of the storage and taxation of grain. Other staple crops dominated in other parts of the world (like rice in East Asia, and maize in the Americas), but it was wheat that fueled the Roman Empire and the Industrial Revolution. Wheat now provides one-fifth of the world’s calories. The fact that it does so is thanks to centuries of human ingenuity and scientific improvement.

Sources indicate that six thousand years ago, when the Sumerian civilization was beginning to emerge in what is now Iraq, human consumption of grain was already ancient history. Remains of domesticated wheat from around 10,000 years ago have been found in Anatolia. These leftovers were wild emmer and einkorn (two progenitors of wheat), which looked a lot like the other wild grasses growing around them: a tall stalk topped by a small seed head. They were variably distributed throughout the landscape, and their seeds ripened at different times, so collecting them would have been laborious. Nonetheless, the people of the ancient Levant found the effort worthwhile, as the seeds were calorie-dense and stored well.

By farming wheat, humans unintentionally made it worse but also improved it. Wild wheat had reproduced without human assistance for millions of years. Its seeds, the grains that we eat, are attached to the head of the plant by a thin stalk called a rachis. When the seeds are mature, the rachis shatters, dispersing the seeds on the ground.

This process is essential for wild wheat to reproduce. Human intervention removed this selection pressure, allowing plants that did not shatter to reproduce. Because nonshattering is a recessive trait, nonshattering plants cannot produce shattering offspring.1 As a result, nonshattering plants proliferated, supplanting their wild predecessors. This is how archaeologists observed that domestication was underway.2.

Recent findings suggest that neolithic farmers collected and planted seeds from the heads of plants that remained intact, whereas seeds that had already fallen to the ground were less likely to be harvested or planted. Stores of emmer and einkorn dated as early as 7600 B.C.E. show rough scars, not the smooth tears left by spontaneous shattering, indicating that the natural reproductive process had been interrupted by harvesters. Once the seed-shattering trait had disappeared, wheat was almost completely dependent on humans collecting and planting its seeds to reproduce. In perhaps a thousand years, millions of years of selection for seed shattering had been undone.

It has been revealed that on the positive side, yields went up. Grains grew bigger thanks to human cultivation. Naturally, grain size varied, but larger grains were less likely to be blown away or slip out of harvesters’ baskets and were therefore overrepresented in the seeds saved and replanted. On top of that, humans tend to plant seeds deeper than they naturally scatter, and larger seeds are more likely to germinate at greater depths. These processes are thought to have increased grain size by a quarter over the first 500 to 1,000 years of cultivation. By this time, wheat could no longer thrive without help from humans. But the transition to agrarian, sedentary communities enabled by bigger harvests also marked the beginning of our dependence on farming.

The next vital step came just as wheat was beginning to spread to surrounding regions, when it absorbed a whole newly introduced set of genes from another species.

One way plants differ from animals is that they can hybridize much more easily, sometimes even happily adding whole fresh genomes to their own. Long before domestication, emmer wheat had already done this: Wild emmer is a naturally occurring amalgam of a cousin of einkorn and another species known as goat grass (Aegilops speltoides). Emmer is therefore tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.

In a recent development, emmer and einkorn wheat diffused throughout Anatolia to Cyprus and beyond as farmers migrated out of the Fertile Crescent. Around this time, emmer hybridized again, incorporating the genome of a second species of goat grass (Aegilops tauschii), bringing its chromosome set count to six. This hybridized wheat, which first appears in the archaeological record in northeastern Turkey around 6000 B.C.E., thrived because it had two valuable traits. First, it was free-threshing. Before this, farmers had to pound grains with a mortar and pestle to free them from their tough outer husks, adding a labor-intensive step to every harvest. Second, this upcoming hybrid had higher gluten content, meaning it could form stronger doughs that hold gas, allowing bread to rise. Initially, this saved labor and enabled tastier food. It is now known as bread wheat, or common wheat, and makes up more than 95% of wheat produced today.

Sources indicate that over the next several millennia, cultivation of bread wheat (and agriculture, more or less) spread throughout Europe and Asia. If a plant failed to grow in its fresh soil or was killed by autumn frosts before reaching maturity, it would be superseded by its better-acclimated relatives. Over thousands of years, incremental changes resulted in countless subtly different local “landrace” populations. Wheat also evolved through further hybridization with closely related plants. This is how we got spelt, which combined the larger grains of bread wheat with the strong shells of emmer, protecting it against the wet and cold and allowing it to thrive further north.

Much of this adaptation was probably incidental, just as early selection for larger seeds and nonbrittle rachises had been. But even in ancient times, careful attention was paid to wheat husbandry and to which varieties thrived in which environments. In 50 B.C.E., the Roman writer Varro advised farmers that “on the threshing-floor the largest and best ears should be placed apart, to furnish the best seed.”3 Long before genetics, farmers understood that good seed begat good crops. This contributed to thousands of years of gradual improvement and specialization.

According to recent reports, the Romans may have been intentionally selecting the best plants, but modern scientific wheat breeding began in western Europe in the 19th century. This dramatically sped up yield improvements. A fortuitously large number of early English estate records have survived, meaning we have data for wheat yields starting from before 1275, at which time farmers were producing around 0.6 metric tons per hectare. This was actually worse than the (continental) Romans, who achieved yields up to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.4 Yields remained approximately flat before the 16th century, when they began increasing (and have not stopped).

From the early 1600s through to 1805, yields in Britain almost doubled, increasing from 0.74 in 1604 to 1.26 metric tons per hectare in 1805.5 Deliberate plant selection contributed to this improvement, but intensive selection — that is, aggressively multiplying the very best strains — didn’t really take off until the second half of the 18th century.

Farmers had always wanted to find high-performing seeds, but now they could buy them. Seedsmen emerged, trading hyperadapted local variants like Red Lammas, a strain popular in the 18th century that was known for thriving in chalky soils and making good-quality flour.

Cereals were substantial business: The original London Corn Exchange6 was built in 1747; the Paris exchange in 1767; Amsterdam had its own Korenbeurs more than a century earlier. From 1765, Britons began importing wheat with the express purpose of finding better varieties, and middlemen living in other countries would send samples of promising grains to contacts in Britain. Yields reflect the results of an increasingly commercialized sector. After stasis for hundreds of years, then steady 2.5% per decade growth in the previous two centuries, yields grew 60% between 1805 and 1865.

In the 19th century, progress was still driven by entrepreneurs, usually curious farmers, rather than scientists. One key innovation, pioneered by Patrick Shirreff in Scotland and John Le Couteur in Jersey, was transitioning from selecting a handful of the best plants to breed from, to selecting the best single individual plant, and multiplying it. They didn’t understand the underlying biology, but the results were clear.

In addition to producing more of the best strains, repeated selection and rebreeding of individuals made the traits of the multiplied strains more consistent from generation to generation. As with shattering seed heads 10,000 years earlier, rebreeding meant undesirable genetic variants were eliminated from the population. Early breeders called this “breeding true,” and though the genetic basis for it was not yet understood, it was important to farmers, who prefer more consistent and predictable crops.

Another key development was the intentional crossing of two plants to create a hybrid. A wheat plant can self-pollinate because it contains both male and female reproductive organs, fertilizing its ovules with its own pollen. The overwhelming majority of wheat plants are produced in this way, and therefore have just one parent, which acts genetically as both mother and father. This process doesn’t produce clones initially because each pollen grain or ovule, even from the same individual, is genetically distinct. But it does result in offspring with extremely limited genetic diversity, which diminishes even further with each successive generation of self-breeding.7.

Recent findings suggest that but sometimes cross-pollination produces plants that come from two parents rather than one. In nature this occurs randomly, but plant breeders deliberately take pollen from one plant and use it to fertilize the ovule of another. Shirreff was a pioneer of this technique, too. The best offspring resulting from these crosses would outperform both parents on some key traits. These high-performing varieties would then be multiplied and the seed sold to farmers.

Industry observers note that these techniques were adopted throughout Europe, where the Vilmorin Seed Organization in France and the Swedish Seed Association in Sweden were among the first to institutionalize cereal breeding. In 1884, The Technology of Bread-Making identified as many as 65 wheat varieties, local and imported, available in English grain markets.

According to recent reports, before the Industrial Revolution, Britain was a largely agricultural nation. But by the end of the 19th century, the population had increased more than sevenfold from about 4 million people in 1600 to 30 million in 1900, and only a tenth of workers were employed in agriculture. This would have been impossible without improvements in agricultural yields. The “dark satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution needed wheat just as much as they needed coal and child labor.

According to recent reports, the pace of improvement increased as researchers began to understand more about genetics and evolution. The discoveries of Darwin (natural selection) and Mendel (the inheritance of simple genetic traits, like seed shattering) were essential to understanding why and how techniques applied over the previous centuries had worked. Also critical were contributions of Wilhelm Johannsen, who untangled how much traits were shaped by genes as opposed to the environment, and Ronald Fisher, the “father of modern statistics,” who figured out the underlying maths. Fisher also showed how continuous traits like height could be determined by the cumulative effect of many individual genes. These insights, around 100 years ago, led to the development and widespread adoption of statistical tools to identify the best seed varieties and to predict how their offspring would perform.

Sources indicate that breeders generated a vast array of latest varieties for testing through a combination of exploration and crossing. Exploration, which was often sponsored by the state, meant collecting seeds from the many unique wheat varieties that had proliferated across the earth since the dawn of time. Britain’s Watkins Landrace Wheat Collection, for example, created in the 1930s, acquired more than 800 wheat cultivars from 32 countries, which could be crossed to create more than 300,000 new hybrid varieties. The USDA had the largest program. Using genetic material from these collections, nurseries would generate crosses for initial testing, multiplying the seeds until there were enough to carry out trials. Trials across several locations allowed researchers to distinguish the effects of genes and environment.

But there were still constraints holding back wheat yields. One was wheat rust, a fungal disease that leaves a characteristic orange-brown powdery residue on plants before shriveling and killing them. Ancient writers knew about this disease: The Romans even had a yearly festival, the Robigalia, in which they performed rituals meant to keep it at bay. In the worst-affected years of the mid-20th century, wheat rust was killing off nearly 20% of American wheat. Breeding programs developed resistant varieties, but any respite was short-lived as the fungus would quickly evolve a new line of attack.

Another was wheat plants “lodging,” or falling over under their own weight. Fertilizer had become much cheaper thanks to the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia from nitrogen gas, developed in 1909. But its usefulness for improving wheat production was limited because although fertilizer could in theory make the plants grow larger than before, applying it would often make the stems collapse, making the wheat unharvestable.

At the time, these problems seemed to show that there were fundamental trade-offs limiting yields. It was assumed that further improvements would be incremental. This fueled worry that there would soon be insufficient food for the growing global population; biologist Paul Ehrlich predicted in 1968 that “in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.”.

These gloomy forecasts turned out to be dead wrong. Between 1950 and 1990, wheat yields in many countries — rich and poor — doubled, as did the yields of other crops: the fastest improvement to farming efficiency ever seen. This explosive growth, enabled by advances in breeding together with mechanization and the wider adoption of fertilizer, is referred to as the “Green Revolution.” Norman Borlaug, an American agronomist often called the father of the Green Revolution, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. In 2009 the director of the World Food Programme mentioned that Borlaug “saved more lives than any man in human history.”.

It has been revealed that borlaug didn’t discover anything newly introduced — he just implemented existing techniques better than anyone had before. In 1944, he joined the Mexican Agriculture Program (an initiative founded and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation) under which he produced about 6,000 new crosses over a decade, a huge quantity at a time when most breeders managed fewer than 200 per year. This quantity was essential to generating the high-performing outliers that could become popular new varieties. It is even more vital when two traits you want (like yield and gluten content) are negatively correlated: The more varieties you test, the likelier you are to find one that bucks the trend, performing well on both.

Industry observers note that rather than approaching yield directly, the program focused on two main limiting factors: wheat rust and lodging. The intensive program of crossing and selecting made it possible to develop varieties that carried several forms of resistance to rust at once, and crossbreeding with Japanese “dwarf” wheat varieties, which were shorter and more robust, produced plants that could be juiced up with fertilizer without collapsing. By the 1960s, Borlaug had produced wheat varieties that had it all: resistance to lodging, multiple resistance to wheat rust, and high yields.

In a recent development, one way this breeding program differed from previous ones was that it was split between two separate regions. The original purpose of this was to squeeze two growing seasons into one year, halving the time it took to produce a new generation. After producing the first generation of offspring in the Toluca highlands, west of Mexico City, Borlaug moved the plants north to the lower-altitude Yaqui Valley, then produced the second generation in time to move back south for the following year. In these stages, selection was crude: Only varieties that failed to germinate or were affected by rust were culled. But later stages of the breeding program included yield trials and statistical selection methods.

In a recent development, alternating between two regions had another, perhaps serendipitous, benefit.8 By advancing candidates that survived in both locations, Borlaug had selected those that could perform well across different environments. Selection for photoperiod-insensitive seeds (those able to mature in both despite differing daylight exposure) meant that varieties developed in Mexico might be successfully grown in other countries, and therefore could be shared across the world. Not all plants, and certainly not all wheat, can be photoperiod insensitive, but varieties tested by the Mexican Agriculture Program were, which may explain why wheat was the first crop to flourish in the Green Revolution. Maize, for example, is so sensitive that breeders operate semi-independent breeding programs for different latitudes.

If Ehrlich was aware of this work when he predicted mass starvation in 1968, he cannot have known its significance. In the mid-1960s, India and Pakistan began importing Borlaug’s newly introduced wheat varieties. One descendant of these imported wheats (called Kalyan Sona or “golden savior”) performed extremely well and became one of the most commonly planted varieties in the region. From 1965 to 1975, wheat yields in India and Pakistan nearly doubled;9 production increased so much and so rapidly that there were shortages of labor for harvest. Over time, other less developed countries followed a similar path.

The next stage of plant breeding was identifying specific genes for the precise properties that farmers wanted. The problem was that genotyping and genome sequencing were expensive and slow. The first genome was sequenced in 1977, but it belonged to a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) with a genome nearly a million times smaller than a human’s. Sequencing the first human genome cost somewhere between $300 million and $3 billion, and was achieved much later. And this was just a diploid human genome. Wheat has a genome five times larger than that, partly because of its three hybridized subgenomes.

Breeders came up with a comparatively quick and dirty solution: marker-assisted selection. Instead of tracking genes directly, they used much cruder tests to find genetic features (“markers”) that correlated with given traits. One technique was restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, in which scientists use enzymes to chop DNA into pieces and then literally measure how long the resulting fragments are by how quickly they are pulled through gel by an electric current. While breeders would not know which genes were responsible for traits, they would know that a trait was correlated with a particular pattern of fragment lengths when cut with a particular enzyme.

Despite the crudeness of the method, it still worked for some traits, especially simple ones like rust resistance, which is often controlled by one or two genes. This allowed farmers and breeders to work out whether a variety was going to be good without going through a whole season of growing, as Norman Borlaug had to. This marker-assisted selection for many crops became routine in the 1990s. Field trials remained key, but most strains were filtered out at the marker identification stage, and few ever made it to the field. At the beginning of the decade, only a few hundred markers were known, but by the end, this had expanded to thousands.

Industry observers note that early marker-assisted selection was of limited use for traits like yield, which are influenced by thousands of genes. But we are no longer restricted to looking at a small number of genetic markers. DNA sequencing costs have decreased by a factor of 100,000 since 2000. Now breeders will often use “genomic selection”: essentially, using the entire genome as a marker and letting statistical software predict which genomes are associated with different traits. Genomic selection can tell us if 500 different genes each contribute 0.2% to a trait where traditional marker-assisted selection would have been useless.

According to recent reports, this has revolutionized the process of plant breeding — if not the outcome.10 Global crop yields continue to increase at a steady rate, reflecting the fact that progress is getting harder to come by. We can now use the same genetic prediction tools for complex traits, like yield, grain quality, and drought tolerance, that we once did for simple ones. At the time Norman Borlaug was working, it took months or years and thousands of wheat plants to evaluate a latest variety’s performance. Today, it can take just days to germinate a seedling and make predictions based on a small leaf sample.

Pessimists would say that wheat domesticated us, that we have spent thousands of years in backbreaking labor serving its reproductive ends. Optimists would argue our coevolution has benefited humanity far more, liberating us from a state of subsistence and creating a caloric surplus to sustain the lives of billions.

Sources indicate that the human species used to live hand to mouth: Virtually all our labor was devoted to growing and harvesting food to fend off starvation. Now, in most developed countries, only a tiny fraction of the population works in agriculture. Wheat’s astonishing success is a crucial part of this change. It is the most widely grown crop on earth, covering 1.5% of the planet’s total land area, and is responsible for one-fifth of the world’s calorie intake. But the amount of labor required to produce those calories has decreased enormously. Since 1900, despite the world’s population increasing more than fourfold, the price of wheat is roughly a quarter of what it was.

Recent findings suggest that that transformation is the result of sustained, incremental improvement to yield, to pathogen resistance, to ease of harvest, to taste, to gluten content, and much more. The advancements came from early farmers unknowingly favoring larger seeds; from finicky varieties that couldn’t handle frost, drought, and other hardships being killed off by the elements; and from breeders making active choices about what traits they wanted to cultivate, increasingly backed by the might of modern science. Today, we can sequence wheat’s entire genome and select for exactly the traits we want. Advances in breeding mean that similar stories can be told for every other major crop and farm animal. Each of us now enjoys the fruits of these advances at every mealtime.

According to recent reports, A lot has changed since the first wheat was farmed in the Fertile Crescent. But Enki is just as correct now as he was thousands of years ago: We would have no Sumer without grain.

Latest Update: ‘Steps’ Director Alyce Tzue On “Punk Rock” Inspirations For ‘Cinderella’ Reimagining

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deadline

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For Alyce Tzue, reimagining Cinderella meant giving its stepsisters the chance to shape their own happily-ever-after.
  • DEADLINE: How did you collaborate with the writers to develop this inclusive reimagining of Cinderella?
  • ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s firm, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Alyce Tzue, reimagining Cinderella meant giving its stepsisters the chance to shape their own happily-ever-after. Netflix’s animated adventure film Steps, co-directed with John Ripa, casts Lilith (Ali Wong) and Margot (Stephanie Hsu) as Asian immigrants in a French-inspired fairytale kingdom, where questions of belonging and privilege shape their search for happiness. Meanwhile, Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) must also learn to confront her own societal complacency and dismantle stereotypes that her inherently kind nature unintentionally upholds. Here with Deadline, Tzue discusses the film’s unique visual style, reworking a traditional fairytale and bringing in newly introduced “punk rock” dimensions. Related Stories News Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL's First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton News Amanda Seyfried Admits She "Told A Lot Of People" About Her 'You Can See Everything' Role: "I'm The Most Indiscreet Person".

DEADLINE: How did you collaborate with the writers to develop this inclusive reimagining of Cinderella? Watch on Deadline.

ALYCE TZUE: It began when Riki Lindhome and Kate Micucci had the idea for the stepsisters’ perspective and pitched it to Amy Poehler’s firm, Paper Kite, which then brought it to Netflix. When I came on board, I made the stepsisters Asian immigrants to a fairytale world. We started with these pillars and bigger concepts that we wanted to honor.

One was these outsider sisters who don’t fit into the box of what you would traditionally see as a protagonist getting their happily-ever-after. That does involve race, but also the traditional feminine archetype that’s super soft-spoken and polite, sings to animals, is pretty, and has that face shape you see in every animated movie. We wanted them to find their unique happily-ever-after.

Sources indicate that there was another idea where we wanted to speak about magic as privilege. Of course, Cinderella has gone through a lot of hardship, but you can also ask, “Well, other people in this world have gone through hardship, too. Why is it this one girl who’s elevated above everyone else and has a fairy godmother, a magic dress and all of that?” That was another concept we wanted to speak to.

RELATED: Director Of Netflix’s ‘Cinderella’ Reimagining Welcomes Movie Going Straight To Streaming — Annecy.

DEADLINE: I want to talk more about the Asian immigrant aspect. From a cultural aspect, what did you want to showcase the most?

Industry observers note that TZUE: I grew up in a small town in Jersey, and I was the only Asian kid in my class. It was a very homogenous white community. I was not only the artist, quiet and nerdy, but I also just felt different. Back then, you couldn’t really quite put it into words. You just felt like, “OK, the stories I had to tell and the way that I dress and the way that I understand the world is just different.”.

I wanted the stepsisters to be these immigrants to a fairytale world who don’t fit the archetype, and the kingdom is full of conformists. The writers and my directing partner, John Ripa, really pushed toward the idea of a blended family where things might seem great at first, but then the world gets in the way.

The world treats difference with fear. Lilith embraces her culture in the beginning, but then when she’s rejected, especially after she shares this very deeply cultural story about the snake lady, she rejects her culture as well. You see very little cultural influence in her costumes in the middle of the movie, but then, through the love of both her sisters, she learns self-acceptance, and you actually see the snake motif return at the end. It reflects my own journey of, “OK, I’m rejected, so I reject parts of myself.” Then, as an adult, there’s this embracing of my roots and my culture again. One way is through this movie, to show how beautiful it is.

Recent findings suggest that DEADLINE: There are a lot of distinct animation and personality styles happening between Lilith, Margot and Cinderella. How did you go about developing this?

According to recent reports, TZUE: We always knew that the character styles would be really, really distinct. We wanted to make Cinderella our own, but she’s definitely inspired by classic princesses, whether from Disney or from a lot of the fairytales we had read about. We loved the French version of Cinderella by Charles Perrault, so her style is very French, and the kingdom is very French-inspired.

Lilith and Margot are both contemporary. We wanted the world to be stuck in a historical period to represent, “Oh, these are the old fairytales.” Lilith is inspired by punk rock like Emei, a Chinese American artist who wrote “The Understudy” with Justin Tranter and Olivia Rodrigo, who we have as a needle drop. Margot is also super eccentric and contemporary in that way. She geeks out on frogs, but she probably would’ve liked manga if it had existed back then. These sisters were really fun because we wanted them to be super relatable from the get-go.

RELATED: All The Songs In Netflix’s ‘Steps’: Olivia Rodrigo To Amanda Seyfried.

DEADLINE: What was the biggest creative challenge in terms of putting the movie together?

According to recent reports, TZUE: The creative challenge, honestly, was how much to include from the canon and how much to break the Cinderella story. One canon moment that gave us so much trouble is actually the stepfather’s death. For Cinderella to be orphaned, you have to kill off the father, but to show them getting together, you have to show the father. The interesting thing is that, from this story’s perspective, you want to be with Lilith the whole time. You want to sympathize with her; you want to show how the world is rejecting her. But the moment you kill off Cinderella’s father, you shift your sympathies toward her. How do you stay mad at Cinderella when her dad just died?

That montage, when you see the girls go from being kids to adults, starts right after Lilith is shut in the storm drain and ends when she becomes an adult. You wouldn’t believe how many times we swapped those events around. There were 20 different versions of that at every screening. It’s kind of surprising, a little puzzle piece that you have to treat with a sort of lightness so it doesn’t shift perspective too much.

DEADLINE: That’s interesting to me, because I was wondering how you would put it together. He dies, and then the stepmom is supposed to be “evil,” but it doesn’t go that way at all. I would have figured that that whole part of the story would be the hardest.

TZUE: Right, she’s not evil, she’s just depressed. We actually did have iterations that explored the stepmother being evil because that’s canon, but it really took a lot of the spotlight away from the sisters. Then you have to dive into, “Oh, it’s because of the mom’s influence that the stepsisters treat Cinderella this way.” That took a lot of real estate and time from the film. To get Lilith driving the story, I think we needed to focus on her and Cinderella.

DEADLINE: What was your favorite moment from the film that made you say: “I can’t believe we did it”?

TZUE: The ending. You know what all the emotions are driving to. I have a personal proof of whether or not a moment is good enough, especially something as important as the ending. If I find myself actually jumping up and down and dancing around the house like, hallelujah, this huge breakthrough moment, if I have a physical, emotional reaction like that, then I’m like, “OK, we got something.”.

In a recent development, I’m talking about going back in time to the storm drain. And then even after that, the ripple effect of kindness. What that real act of kindness enables the world to do, and where that leads, is a huge breakthrough for us. If we didn’t have that anchor, I think things would still shift for longer. We would still be trying to find the right ending.

RELATED: ‘Steps’ Voice Cast Guide: Who Voices Who In The Netflix Animated Fairytale Retelling?

Recent findings suggest that DEADLINE: Let’s get into the cast. You have a stacked cast. Let’s talk about Ali Wong and Stephanie Hsu and then Amanda Seyfried.

TZUE: Let me start with Ali, she’s been attached for a long while. She was the first one to join, and it was a no-brainer. We knew that Lilith had to have a spiky exterior, be hilarious and witty, and have a contemporary flavor. Ali Wong was our dream casting, so we went out to her and her only. She brought so much commentary on society and a mature take on a character who’s kind of like, “I hate this kingdom. I can see that they’re biased against me, and I totally get it. I’m going to make jokes about how the prince has been engaged to his fifth cousin since he was born.”.

Then we have Amanda Seyfried, who is just incredible. We valued her so much because she takes on roles and immediately humanizes them. It’s hard for her to take on a role and make it one-dimensional. With Cinderella, especially as a legendary, iconic fairy-tale character, we needed someone who could give her many layers and allow us to sympathize with her as a fully human person. That involves her trauma, her own walls, and her people-pleasing. I thought Amanda delivered amazingly on that front.

Industry observers note that and Stephanie Hsu can do it all. She’s so versatile, and I want her in more comedic roles because Margot is such a boisterous, effusive wild child. Stephanie had a lot of fun with it.

DEADLINE: Young Mazino’s character is a cute, emo troll. Can you talk about his journey into the story?

Industry observers note that TZUE: Once we broke the Cinderella story, we wanted to have a lot of fun with the idea that we had broken out of the constraints of traditional storytelling and were in a fantasy world outside the kingdom. We asked, “What other fairytale tropes could we play with?” The trolls under the bridge were interesting, and we wanted to have more action in the movie. So because of that, we have this society of trolls that don’t belong in either world, sort of like Lilith. We asked, “Can we make a character who resonates with her predicament, in that he also has emotional walls? Can you physicalize it? Can it be a literal mech that he’s in, like, ‘Oh, I don’t belong, so I’m going to protect myself in an actual mechanical creature’?” That’s where Gef came along.

We also wanted to make him super unattractive in his troll society, but beauty’s in the eye of the beholder. For humans, he’s super hunky and hot. We have so many talented writers. In the writers’ room, we were spitballing, and people laughed a lot at the idea of a super-hot troll. That’s where we got Gef from, and Young Mazino was perfect because Ali recommended him. We needed someone who had deadpan humor and a deep, monotone voice.

DEADLINE: And you’ve got Daniel Radcliffe as well. You mentioned earlier that it was a challenge of where to stay or stray from the Cinderella lore. How did you all decide to create The Prince?

Recent findings suggest that TZUE: The Prince is a great opportunity to poke fun at some of the holes in the original story. One of the biggest ones was, “Well, how do you dance with a girl so close and then completely forget what she looks like, so much so that you have to fit a slipper on every woman’s foot in the kingdom?” That’s why we play with the idea of face blindness.

We knew we had to make him a little dumb, so we needed an actor who earns your sympathy above all else. The Prince is so charming and really shows you that he’s trying his best, but isn’t the sharpest tool in the toolbox. We were so lucky to get Daniel Radcliffe. He’s very picky with his roles, but he knocks it out of the park.

DEADLINE: What were some directorial inspirations you drew from, either in style or in how you shaped the story?

TZUE: We pulled inspiration from quite a few live-action films. I personally love Joe Wright’s Pride and Prejudice. He tackles the intimacy of sisters so well. Some of those closer camera angles when the sisters are bonding, the rack focuses from one girl to the other, a lot of the lighting on the streets—anything that feels romantic. We also drew from movies like Little Women by Greta Gerwig and Marie Antoinette by Sofia Coppola, which was a massive one as well, because she infused the Rococo era with a lot of contemporary flavor and made the whole movie feel so delicious, from the pastries and colors to the pastels. We wanted to go maximalist, and that movie gave us a lot of inspiration.

💡 Key Takeaways
