What’s the difference between an automatic and manual espresso machine — and the one an ex-barista recommends

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime.
  • According to recent reports, but the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy.
  • Recent findings suggest that what type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that coffee can feel like an overwhelming pastime. There's so much noise online about coffee — grind size, flow rate, milk texture — that I'm surprised any newbies are brave enough to take the plunge and buy their first espresso machine.

According to recent reports, but the most important difference is the type of espresso machine you buy. There are loads of different types of machines for different types of coffee drinkers: superautomatic, semi-automatic, manual, bean-to-cup/all-in-one... the list goes on. Today, let's get to the bottom of it.

Recent findings suggest that what type of espresso machine is best for you, and which should you buy? I'm using Casabrews, Ninja, and De'Longhi espresso machines to exemplify my points today — and they're all on sale for Black Friday.

The De'Longhi Rivelia is my favorite automatic espresso machine. It has two hoppers so you can switch out beans if you so please, and it makes both hot and cold drinks at the push of a button (but you have to buy the cold frother separately, unfortunately).

The Casabrews 3700 Essential is the best espresso machine under $100 (of the ones I've tested). This machine makes delicious coffee, and while you need to spend a little time learning how to use it, it's totally worth it.

Sources indicate that the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is like the best of all worlds. It has a built-in grinder and tamping assist to prevent messes, and it has both manual and automatic milk frothing. This machine is great for learning how to be a barista.

It has been revealed that there's one key difference between automatic and manual machines: ease of use. (Size and price also come into play!).

Automatic machines are called that for a reason: press a button, and you get hot coffee in seconds.

An automatic coffee machine selection screen generally looks something like this.

Sources indicate that some machines have upwards of 50 recipes. The De'Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499) offers 38 recipes — some of which I, an ex-barista, had never heard of — including hot and cold beverages. At the press of a button, the machine makes your drink for you.

Depending on price, some automatic machines have integrated milk frothing, like the pictured De'Longhi Rivelia ($1,499) or the De'Longhi Magnifica Duo ($999).

In a recent development, you don't have to do anything. No grinding, no tamping, no calculating dosage volume. As long as there are beans in the hopper, water in the tank, and electricity in the machine, it'll take care of everything.

Automatic machines are ideal if you drink a lot of coffee, but either you don't have time to make it yourself, or you don't want to make it yourself. Both are valid.

But what about a manual espresso machine? Manual espresso machines vary in functionality — some have built-in grinders, so closer to automatics, but some are incredibly hands-on. Let's run through a few examples.

This is the Casabrews 3700 Essential. It's the cheapest espresso machine I've rated highly, and my only recommendation for a sub-$100 espresso machine. If you want the cheapest manual espresso machine on the market, I'd go for this one.

Recent findings suggest that this machine necessitates either a separate grinder or getting your coffee ground for espresso at a local cafe. It comes with dual-walled (pressurized) coffee baskets. While a pressurized basket means it doesn't make "technically" perfect espresso, it's a fantastic machine to learn on, as it's incredibly forgiving.

According to recent reports, however, you do need to spend a bit of time learning the ropes. Unlike an automatic machine, you have to do everything yourself. You need to grind the coffee, put the coffee in the portafilter, press "start", and steam your milk.

If you want to get into coffee as a hobby, or you like the routine of making coffee, then I would recommend a manual machine such as this.

However, if you want to make your life easier and you have a little more money to spend, I'd also recommend looking at manual espresso machines with built-in grinders, like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

As you can see, this machine has a lot more going on than the Casabrews 3700 Essential. The Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus has a built-in grinder (on the left) and tamping assist (also on the left).

Although you still need to put beans in the hopper and adjust grind size yourself, this machine takes a lot of the hassle out of your morning brew. The Luxe Cafe Mini doesn't have automatic milk frothing, but the Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (pictured) does. The Mini will set you back $449, while the Plus goes for $499. Right now, though, the Mini Plus is $419, and the Mini is $399.

Industry observers note that the long and short of it is this: No time to spend making coffee? Just want coffee, stat? Automatic — De'Longhi Rivelia.

Want to learn the art of coffee, and don't mind buying a grinder or getting your beans ground at a cafe? Manual — Casabrews 3700 Essential.

In a recent development, still want to make the coffee yourself, but you want a built-in grinder? Manual with a built-in grinder — Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus.

Recent findings suggest that although not as integral as ease of use, size is also something to consider. In general, automatic machines are pretty huge. Here's a size comparison of our three case studies.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus (manual, grinder).

Casabrews 3700 Essential (manual, no grinder).

If you're short on space, the answer's kind of obvious — it should probably be a manual with no grinder. However, you need to remember you will either require a separate grinder or have to get your beans ground at a cafe.

Obviously, though, automatic machines are much larger than manuals. I would only recommend automatics if you're sure you have the space for them — they look bigger and bulkier than the numbers might suggest.

For everyone in between, I'd go for the Ninja.

Obviously, the more features a machine has, the higher its price. In general, automatic machines will set you back at least $1,000 — the only models I've tested under this are the $999 De'Longhi Magnifica Duo and the $999 Jura ENA4 — the latter of which can't make milk drinks. Honestly, what's the point? If you like black coffee, just get a drip machine like the Moccamaster KBGV Select ($270 right now on Black Friday deal).

Industry observers note that after automatic machines come manual machines with built-in grinders. This price can range from $3,000 (Breville Oracle Dual Boiler) to $229 (Amzchef Espresso Machine with Grinder). As someone who's tested all the cheapest models and all the high-end models, I would be wary of a machine charging less than $400. I'd recommend machines like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini (pictured, $499), Breville Barista Express ($699), and De'Longhi Arte Evo ($699) — the latter of which can make cold(ish) brew!

I want you to answer these three questions.

To help you out, I made a quiz!

What did you get? Here are my top recommendations for each type.

In a recent development, depending on your quiz results, I'd recommend one of these three machines. Let me know which one you go for in the comments — I'd love to hear about it!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) released earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

In a recent development, with AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

Industry observers note that this expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company states this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

Sources indicate that I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the upcoming speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that customers are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield.
  • Sources indicate that in the first half, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. #200058. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3525 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Recent findings suggest that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell claims. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

It has been revealed that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

It has been revealed that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

It has been revealed that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team revealed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

According to recent reports, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

It has been revealed that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

In a recent development, sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just substantial enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

In a recent development, but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson indicates. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

Industry observers note that in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

It has been revealed that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Industry observers note that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more notable than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell indicates. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Sources indicate that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Recent findings suggest that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu states.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” states neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra indicates, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Recent findings suggest that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra indicates. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell claims. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Sources indicate that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell claims. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy declared US $62 million in newly introduced funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

According to recent reports, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Industry observers note that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Sources indicate that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”.

Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.

Apple Newton was Appleâs PDA released in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

Sources indicate that palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palmâs mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

It has been revealed that style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

It has been revealed that taligent was a troubled software tech giant, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

Industry observers note that webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

Sources indicate that does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6, and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Denmark’s TV2 has dipped into the independent production market for an Acting Program Director as it seeks penance for the scandal around Truman Show-like reality series Everybody Loves Rasmus.

Sune Roland will take up the position on December 1, and will lead the TV2 programming division during a period the network “is working to rebuild the Danish public’s trust.” Given his position is an acting role, it’s not certain he will be TV2’s long-term program chief just yet.

In a recent development, the follows the departures of Content Director Ulla Pors and Program Director Dorthe Thirstrup following the disastrous launch of Alle Elsker Rasmus (Everybody Loves Rasmus). Related Stories News Content Chiefs At Denmark's TV2 Step Down To "Restore Trust" After Backlash Over 'Truman Show'-Style Reality Series News Banijay Takes On Norway's 'The Comedy League'.

It has been revealed that the show faced immense public backlash for duping comedian Rasmus Wallbridge into believing his dream film concept was being produced. It was scrapped soon after launch, and TV2’s directors have rolled out an investigation into how the show was greenlit in the first place. Their response has been fast and decisive during in an almost unprecedented situation for a major European broadcaster. Watch on Deadline.

Roland is a former TV2 exec, having risen as high as Head of Content, and returns after four years in the independent production sector. He had worked as Managing Director of Strong Productions, the Fremantle Denmark production house that merged with Blu last year. Following his exit there, he launched his own company, Shift Studios.

Frederik Lauesen, who was installed as Acting Content Director at TV2 in the aftermath of the scandal, noted: “I am very pleased that Sune Roland has agreed to take on the role of Acting Programme Director. Sune brings extensive experience; he is well-liked and respected within the industry and possesses a deep understanding of both TV 2 and the Danish production landscape. He is a highly skilled professional and an accomplished leader, and we will greatly benefit from his expertise in the time ahead.”.

Industry observers note that lauesen mentioned TV2 was facing “a serious situation” and that rebuilding trust was paramount. “We must address this while continuing to manage a large and diverse portfolio of content – an effort we carry out in close collaboration with our talented colleagues in the programming department and the Danish production industry. Sune’s experience from both sides of the table will prove valuable in the time ahead.”.

Industry observers note that roland acknowledged he was joining in “particularly challenging times,” but added: TV2 holds a special place for me, and I know how many talented and dedicated people work every day to create content that truly matters to the Danish public. I look forward to contributing my experience and collaborating with both colleagues and production companies.”.

It has been revealed that roland worked as TV2’s Head of Factual between 2007 and 2011, and then from 2012 until 2022 held roles such as Head of Programming, Channel Head, and Head of Content. He has also held senior leadership positions at Koncern TV and Metronome Productions.

TV2 will begin a recruitment process for a “future leadership team within the programming division” at a later date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that walmart appears to have dropped support for Apple Pay on its website and in its iPhone app. This comes just a few weeks after the retailer finally added support for Apple’s payment platform to its app and website.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

It has been revealed that appleosophy spotted the change last week. There’s no indication whether the feature was removed deliberately or if this is some sort of bug.

In the “Payment method” section of the checkout page on Walmart’s app and website, it no longer lists Apple Pay as an accepted payment method where it previously did. Not only that, but it doesn’t show up under the “Other ways to pay” or “More ways to pay” sections of the checkout page either.

Walmart still accepts Apple Pay in its retail stores. The retailer began rolling out contactless payment support in August, including Apple Pay, Google Pay, contactless cards, and more. For years, Walmart refused to support Apple Pay, instead trying (and failing) to convince shoppers to use its own Walmart Pay platform.

It has been revealed that we’ll update this post if Walmart comments on Apple Pay’s disappearance from its website and app. Hopefully, it’s a bug that the firm fixes sooner rather than later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

Recent findings suggest that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.
